utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We will hear, in the coming days, the final argument of the parties in this case. Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to start, I have a few matters which I'd like to raise. First, the Cermak and Markac Defence are invited to file their public redacted versions of their final briefs as soon as possible. The Gotovina Defence has filed its redacted version. Then, I'd like to read a statement on behalf of the Chamber on sentencing submissions. The Chamber will now address the parties' submissions on sentencing. In its final brief, paragraph 589, the Cermak Defence requests that it be granted an opportunity to address the Chamber orally regarding sentencing, should the Chamber find Cermak guilty of any of the charges. Its request notwithstanding, the Cermak Defence addresses sentencing in its final brief with the exception of the gravity of the offence and the totality of the conduct. The Markac Defence objects to the Tribunal's practice of pronouncing on the accused's guilt and issuing a sentence at the same time. This objection can be found in paragraph 284 of the Markac Defence's final briefly. The Markac Defence does not seek any relief in this regard and notwithstanding its objection makes submissions on sentencing in its final brief. The original version of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence provided for separate guilt and sentencing proceedings. This was abandoned in 1998 with the adoption of Rule 87(C), establishing a combined guilt and sentencing phase. This new practice is also reflected in Rule 86(C) which sets out that the parties shall also address matters of sentencing in closing arguments. The Chamber finds no reason to deviate from this practice in the present case. Therefore, the Cermak Defence's request is denied. In light of this decision, if the Cermak Defence and the Markac Defence wish to make any further submissions on sentencing, they have the opportunity to do so during their closing arguments. In its final brief, the Gotovina Defence indicated that it chose not to make any submissions on sentencing. Although the Chamber takes it that this position has been adopted after careful consideration, it does not consider it to be binding, and therefore the Gotovina Defence is not deprived of the opportunity to make oral submissions on sentencing as part of its closing argument, if it should wish to do so. And this concludes the Chamber's statement on the parties' sentencing submissions. Finally, in relation to the closing arguments, the Prosecution has six hours to deliver its closing arguments. Defence teams each have two and a half hours to deliver their closing arguments. And as the Chamber indicated earlier, the Defence teams may divide their time for closing arguments amongst themselves as they see fit. The Prosecution has one hour for rebuttal arguments and the Defence teams have one hour in total for rejoinder arguments. These are the practical arrangements the parties are aware of. Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to present its final arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Learned colleagues for the Defence, and all those in the courtroom and in the booths. Your Honours, I will speak first for the Prosecution, discussing the JCE, its common purpose to forcibly displace Serbs, its members, including General Gotovina, General Cermak and General Markac, and its means, including unlawful shelling attacks and destruction and looting. Mr. Russo will discuss in more detail the artillery attacks and the resulting deportation and forcible transfer of Croatian Serbs. Mr. Hedaraly will then speak about the crimes committed against Croatian Serbs and against Croatian Serb property. Ms. Gustafson, Mr. Carrier, and Ms. Mahindaratne, the latter two who will be joining us for the submissions later will discuss the contributions to the JCE and the individual criminal responsibility of Generals Gotovina, Cermak, and Markac, respectively. Your Honours, on the 4th of August, 1995, Croatian military forces commenced Operation Storm to retake territory that had been under Croatian Serb control since 1991, including Sector South. Towns and villages, including Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, were placed under artillery fire beginning at 0500 hours. The people who lived there, and international observers who witnesses those attacks, realised as they were happening that they were directed at civilians and civilian areas, that it was the civilian towns and villages themselves that were under attack, that no place was safe. What they didn't know was that the attack on their towns and villages was the result of an order from General Gotovina which specified that, in addition to communication centres and command posts, the towns themselves should be shelled. And what those terrified civilians also didn't know was that the order to shell the towns had resulted from a meeting of the Supreme Commander of Croatian forces Franjo Tudjman and his top military advisors, including General Gotovina, General Markac, Minister of Defence Susak and others, about, among other things, the importance of producing civilian flight through shelling. That objective succeeded and President Tudjman was able to say shortly after, referring to the fact that most of the Serbs were gone, "what we have created just now is a Croat state which will last for centuries." That's P467, page 2. And after the successful completion of this aspect of the operation and the flight of most of the Serbs, President Tudjman and other officials implemented measures and willfully failed to implement other necessary measures in order to ensure that Serbs would not return in sufficient number to again represent a demographic threat. As Serb homes and farms were destroyed and pillaged by General Gotovina's and General Markac's men, among others, and many Serb civilians were killed, a climate of impunity prevailed. Croatian officials, particularly, General Cermak, who was personally installed by President Tudjman to handle the Knin area, deflected inquiries and denied the crimes, attempted to limit and control access and reporting by internationals and media, collected hundreds of bodies without accompanying investigations, and failed to institute the necessary preventative or punitive measures to stop the crimes they were denying. President Tudjman and other officials also erected administrative barriers to ensure that Serbs would not return in meaningful number, and initiated areas to repopulate the areas from which Serbs had fled not with returning Serbs but with ethnic Croats, and thus cement the demographic transformation that would, as noted earlier, ensure a Croat state that would last for centuries. The Defence has argued, among other things that "Croatia" had no plan or policy to expel the Serb population but "instead" was a victim of Serbian aggression and wanted to reintegrate its territories peacefully as evidenced by the Vance Plan. Now it should be noted first that no one is alleging that Croatia had a plan or policy to expel. It was the members of the JCE. Further, there is no dispute that the Croatian people suffered from terrible crimes committed by Serbian forces. But there is likewise no conflict between that victimisation and the plan to expel Serbs. They coexist logically and factually in an all too common tragic cycle of victimisation. And the fact that President Tudjman agreed to the Vance Plan at a time when Croatia had not yet built its army and when one-third of its territory was controlled by Krajina Serbs tells us little about President Tudjman's concerns and objectives when Croatia had become militarily powerfully and the opportunity arose, in his own words, to be bold and pay them back. And that reference you'll see at P461, page 11. The General Gotovina Defence devotes considerable attention in its brief to the crimes committed by Serb forces against Croats, to the support the Krajina Serbs received from other Serbs, to the unsuccessful negotiations to reintegrate the Krajina, and to the various military operations that preceded and followed Operation Storm. Some of that lengthy section is intended to buttress the argument that Serbian flight resulted from an RSK evacuation decision and that the flight of tens of thousands of Serbs had nothing to do with the unlawful shelling attack. Your Honours, as you will hear in more detail from Mr. Russo, this argument not only ignores the relationship between the evacuation decision and the unlawful shelling attack, but, more importantly, ignores the evidence that the shelling was a primary cause of flight for many persons, including those who never heard of the evacuation decision or who fled before the decision or who made their minds up to flee because of the shelling or who were convinced to follow others who were leaving, because the shelling made it clear to them that they had no other choice. And you will find such references in the final brief at paragraph 616 through 618, 623 through 624, 626, 629, and 641. Now the Defence backdrop section also casts United Nations personnel as enemies bent on undermining Croatia and suggests that therefore their reports should be regarded or disregarded as mere propaganda. A reference seen at paragraph 119 of the Gotovina brief. In part, these characterisations conflate UN decisions and actions in Bosnia, where difference circumstances prompted different decisions. Ironically, the Defence brief attacks the United Nations for passivity in Bosnia and then, for subsequent decisions, to stand firm on its mission in Croatia. Additionally, it attaches, inaccurately, ill motives to such decisions. For example, Operation Active Presence is cast as an effort to purposefully place in harm's way UN troops in order to trigger international condemnation of Croatia's military offensive. But the citation for that proposition reveals that the UN considered the alternative to remaining in position either impracticable or more likely to provoke action against UN personnel and, therefore, made a decision which it believed reduced the likelihood of the very circumstances that the Defence accuses them of trying to create. Similarly, Your Honours, the Defence inflates and mischaracterises events in Sector South preceding Storm. Thus, General Forand's evidence that he knew of one unit which sold fuel and stopped it as soon as he found out, is conflated with a comment that Hill heard from someone that some sectors had sold fuel in large amounts, and is thus falsely attributed to Sector South, UNCRO. Alun Roberts is condemned, when the citations are checked, for such transgressions as failing to put the name RSK in quotation marks or for "trying to describe two-sided violations of the agreement, the responsibility of the Croatian side and of the rebel Serbs." That's found at footnote 92 and D1344. Most obviously, Your Honours, the attempt to suggest that UN personnel were biased in favour of Serbs and therefore provided evidence consistent with that view is not supported by the actual attitudes of UN personnel whom the Court had an opportunity to meet. As well as some of the reasons why they would not be supporters of the RSK. For example, the very statement of Hill about the fuel also makes clear the problems that UNCRO had with Serbian officials, including being held at gunpoint. And that's P292, page 7. Your Honours, on the heels of some of the references I just mentioned, it should be noted that the Prosecution has found numerous citations in Defence briefs that do not support the proposition for which they are cited or that do not accurately reflect the exhibit or transcript. We're not suggesting that this was purposeful. Merely urging the Court to examine carefully any citations upon which it may wish to rely, whether Defence or Prosecution. And the same is true for legal citations. For example, the Defence cites Blaskic for the proposition that a Trial Chamber cannot draw adverse inferences from circumstantial evidence where there are factual inconsistencies, that is paragraph 152, and indeed, cites it throughout the brief, including in support of the position that the existence of prohibitory orders precludes the Court from drawing adverse inferences about the accused's responsibility from such factors as the scale of the crimes. This interpretation is incorrect. Blaskic established no specific or new rule regarding circumstantial evidence but merely applied the standard rule which does not provide, as the Defence suggests, that any actual inconsistencies preclude an adverse finding. Instead, that rule requires the Court to determine from the totality of evidence whether a reasonable alternative is made out from the evidence overall. Thus, in the context of orders, the Milutinovic Trial Chamber found that the "manifest insufficiency" of orders against crimes, in view of the wide-spread criminality known to an accused, was an indication of his shared intent in the JCE and a means by which he significantly contributed to it through creation and maintenance of a climate of impunity. That's Milutinovic, paragraph 772, 777, through 78 and 782. Finally, with respect to the Defence's backdrop section, its express purpose is identified in its conclusion at paragraph 142, which states that the Trial Chamber cannot conclude that Croatia was pursuing a policy of expelling its Serb population by launching an unnecessary war, and thus, no adverse inference can be made as to the purpose or objective of Operation Storm and subsequent events. The Defence therefore spends a great deal of effort debunking an argument that has never been made. To the contrary, the Prosecution has made clear from the start that it did not assert that the mere fact that Operation Storm was undertaken was to be taken as evidence of criminal intent for the charges in the indictment. So, again, Croatia's decision to conduct a military operation -- So I will say again, as we said in the opening. Croatia's decision to conduct a military operation to retake the Krajina is not at issue. What is at issue is the successful effort undertaken by certain officials, including the three accused, to use that circumstance to eliminate much of the Serb presence in the Krajina. The fact that Storm was going to be launched and the confidence of Croatian military and political leaders that the Krajina would be successfully retaken, based in part on Croatia's new military prowess, its string of recent victories and President Tudjman's certitude that Milosevic would not intervene with the VJ meant that there was an opportunity not only to finally reintegrate Croatian territory within its internationally recognised borders, but also, as President Tudjman saw it, to ensure the long-term existence of the state. President Tudjman, the undisputed political and military leader of Croatia, and a man devoted to the vision of an enduring Croatian state resurrected from the past, was convinced that multi-ethnic countries were not sustainable and that nations should be as ethnically homogeneous as possible. That's P444, paragraph 31. To him, this was so indisputable that he made no attempts to hide his views, even lecturing dignitaries from multi-cultural nations about this danger. And that is found at P452, Your Honour, and at transcript 4936 through 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you slow down four per cent while reading, then the French interpreters will be able to follow you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the context of Croatia, this referred to Serbs whom President Tudjman regarded as belonging to a different civilisation and who didn't belong together with Croats; P444, paragraphs 32, and P452. In his eyes, Croatia represented the border between the east and west, a buffer preventing Orthodox incursion from the east. That's P452, page 9. This perception that Serbs were of a different civilisation, a foreign body, was also reflected in comments by Tudjman or his Chief of Staff, Sarinic, that Serbs were a cancer on the stomach of Croatia; P444. Or that after Storm, Serbs would no longer "spread cancer which has been destroying Croatian national being in the middle of Croatia and didn't allow Croatian people to be truly alone on its own." P473, page 3. Or that Serbs in Croatia were a "potential Trojan horse." P465, page 12. Or a potential "bomb in our hands." P468, page 14. In short, President Tudjman believed that Serbs were too numerous in Croatia and constituted a strategic threat for that reason. P444, paragraph 31. And the answer to this danger was to move them elsewhere. President Tudjman spoke very approvingly of population transfers to achieve ethnic homogeneity. See P444, paragraph 31. And on that, key members of the Croatian leadership saw eye to eye with Serbian national leaders from the beginning. In January 1992, during a discussion about "lasting solutions" based on the "homogeneity of certain areas," see P459, pages 4 and 13, President Tudjman told Bosnian Serb leader Koljevic that "wherever national problems so conceived emerged as they did with us ... that was brought to a conclusion by exchanges." P459, page 32. More than three and a half years later, Sarinic reported to Tudjman about two recent meetings with Milosevic, during which Sarinic conveyed to Milosevic that the fewer Serbs in Croatia and Croats in Serbia, the better for future relations, reminding Milosevic of the demographic changes after World War II and suggesting that it was not necessary to use "big words" like ethnic cleansing. P465, page 12. So when President Tudjman gathered in Brioni on the 31st of July with his top military advisors, who were confident that they could quickly prevail over the outnumbered, ill-equipped and overstretched Serbs, and he listened to their detailed logistical and tactical proposals, President Tudjman noted that "there is something still missing." P461, page 10. And went on to remind them of several things. He urged them to remember how many Croatian villages and towns had been destroyed but that this was still not the situation in Knin; 461, page 10. But now, he noted, they had the "pretext" to strike Knin with artillery. Page 10. Noting that there would be great panic anyway once the offensive began, President Tudjman called for an exit route from Knin "because it is important that those civilians set out, and then the army will follow them, and when the columns set out, they will have a psychological effect on each other." Page 15 of 461. It was, as President Tudjman said, time to be bold. The importance of getting civilians out was underscored by proposals for the use of psychological operations, psy-ops, to ensure their flight. Miroslav Tudjman, President Tudjman's son and the head of military intelligence, and President Tudjman proposed radio broadcasts stating that civilians are leaving, telling them which direction to head in "so we have as little to do as possible." 461, page 23. A bit later in the discussion, Minister of Defence Susak suggested dropping leaflets, "instilling the feeling among them that you have succeeded, that you are above them, that you are dropping leaflets, this will provoke something." 461, page 29. Now this would simultaneously advance the objective while assuaging international concerns. As President Tudjman noted, "This means giving them a way out, while ostensibly guaranteeing them civil rights, et cetera." Followed, as you will recall, by a little chuckle. Later, Susak expressed great satisfaction about the effect of the electronic warfare in causing Serbs to leave. That is transcript 4192 through 93. And indeed, this successful approach was replicated in a later operation in Bosnia, during which the HV, under General Gotovina, disseminated leaflets which pretended to be an order from the Bosnian Serb army telling Serb civilians to flee. That's P1113, page 464. The Defences argue that there is no evidence that any leaflet was either received by or directed at any Serb civilian. Even if accurate, Your Honours, this would not change the focus at the Brioni meeting on causing civilian flight. But, in any event, as you will hear in more detail from Mr. Russo, it is not accurate. And as you will hear in great detail in further submissions, the gap that President Tudjman pointed out between the Croat towns and villages that had been attacked and as yet untouched Knin was bridged by the bold action he called for. You will hear about the order to put Knin and other towns under shelling and the unlawful attack that followed. That will be addressed in more detail by Mr. Russo, so I'd now like to move on to another aspect of the common purpose, burning and destruction. Your Honours, as the evidence reveals and as you will hear in more detail from Mr. Hedaraly, the devastation of Serbian property as well as attacks on Serbian civilians began almost immediately and persisted throughout the indictment period. The Defence has asserted that there is no express statement in the Brioni meeting about achieving the common purpose through crimes such as plunder or wanton destruction, and no evidence that would allow for an inference that there was a common purpose to commit such crimes. But what needs to be enunciated or expressed at any given moment is dependant upon context. Some things do not need to be said to be readily understood. The Defence itself has underscored the extent of crimes committed by Serbs against Croats prior to Storm and the number of people affected. That awareness alone would inform any discussion about sending troops into the very area that symbolised that victimisation about the inevitably of vengeful criminal acts of the absence of meaningful preventative measures. And that was only underscored by General Gotovina's reminder of the troops under his command who were literally from that area. That's at P461, page 10. But even if that factor was not as pronounced as the Defence itself has insisted, the Brioni meeting took place immediately after Croatian troops burned and looted Grahovo. Virtually all units were involved and "the entire Grahovo was on fire." P71, pages 49 through 50. And the awareness of these crimes was reflected in the very orders that preceded and accompanied Storm and which the Defence has again underlined. So the Defence acknowledges, albeit indirectly, that the prospect of burning and looting in the absence of meaningful preventative measures was apparent to those at Brioni as they discussed the forced departure of the Serb civilian population. But the Defence argues that it was precisely those orders, as well as orders that followed, that contradicted any intention for the crimes to occur. They suggest that the issuance of orders by "the entire Croatian leadership, civilian and military" renders it patently absurd to conclude that there was no genuine intent to implement them. The significance of such orders, however, as the Milutinovic Chamber has recognised, cannot be understood in the abstract. The intent behind them must be measured against such factors as the scale, duration, and gravity of the crimes, the extent of the real efforts to curtail them, and the overall objectives of those who issued them. When orders are reissued to soldiers who have just committed crimes with impunity, when hundreds of bodies are collected without accompanying investigation, when the crimes are denied, when the arrests or detentions dictated by the massive crimes - but that would expose the denials as untrue - do not take place, when those who might expose the crimes are kept away from the area or threatened, when satisfaction is taken from the results of the crimes, when the totality, Your Honours, of the evidence is considered, the lack of genuine intent to implement such orders is exposed. And, in any event, even if there was insufficient evidence that the common purpose included looting and burning, it is clear based on the above that the attacks on Serb property - the burning and looting - were natural and foreseeable consequences of an effort to force Serbs from the Krajina, just as were the killings and inhumane treatment against Serb civilians and therefore fall within JCE 3. There is, therefore, no issue of an extended or expanded JCE as the Defence has suggested. Ambassador Galbraith, who met regularly with the Croatian leadership, who received information from many sources about the extensive and systematic destruction of Serb property and crimes against Serbs, and who constantly raised the issue with the Croatian leadership, testified that these crimes could not have taken place without the acquiescence of Croatia's leadership. And you will see a portion of that testimony, Your Honours, on screen: "These were serious and systematic crimes for which the Croatian leadership is fully responsible. Given the disciplined nature of the army and the leadership was fully in command and had full power to prevent, these were crimes committed on orders, or it was a matter of state policy to tolerate or encourage them." That's P444 at paragraph 46. The Defence insists that, to the contrary, other internationals "repeatedly stated that they did not believe that the looting and burning was part of a government plan." It is instructive to look briefly at the testimony they cite and, in particular, the testimony of PW-AG18. And with that in mind, Your Honours, may we move into private sessions for approximately 30 to 60 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thus, Your Honours, this witness didn't contradict Galbraith. He corroborated him. The principle difference is that Galbraith named those who sought a more radical approach to the national problem and they were the very top leadership: President Tudjman, Minister Susak, in particular. A position that is confirmed by numbers of Presidential transcripts that the Court has seen. This is also wholly consistent with the testimony of Special Rapporteur Rehn, who testified that she had no doubt that the crimes committed by Croatian forces were pursuant to orders or silent approval; P598, page 8. As for the proposition that orders belie intent, Ambassador Galbraith was presented with that proposition. He was asked by the Defence, after he testified that he had been told of orders to stop the crimes, if there were orders being given to stop the burning of houses, then permitting those criminal activities was not state policy, was it? That's at transcript 5077 through 78. And Ambassador Galbraith explained: "I do not agree with -- with what you've just stated. I have enough experience over the years that I served in Croatia with Croatian officials and Serb officials giving orders and saying that they'd given orders that they had -- and making promises they had no intention of keeping, and I do not believe that the Croatian government made a serious attempt to bring this destruction under control until such time as it was basically -- there was nothing left for the Serbs to return to." And that's at transcript 5078. The reference we've heard to persons in the Croatian government structure who did not share the radical approach to the national problem but who were nevertheless unable or unwilling to change the passivity or inaction also provides insight into the suggestion by the Defence that it is absurd to suggest that everyone who issued an order must have done so without any intention that it be followed. With the key members of the leadership committed to ensuring a permanent removal of Serbs, it is unlikely that others would generate the will to overcome that position or, in any event, be able to effectively counteract it, if they did. Recall, for example, that the chief of military police administration, Lausic explained that maintaining military discipline is first and foremost the task of the commanders. That's P2159 at paragraph 21. And, as he reminded colleagues even before the commencement of Storm, if commanders did not do this job, even huge numbers of military police would not be able to prevent crimes. D45, transcript 15257 through 58. When the Supreme Commander and the top military commander of the district share the purpose of forcing Serbs from the Krajina, the prospect of impacting or reversing the climate of impunity is meager. I should also note that the Defence effort to suggest that the discipline or law and order responsibilities of persons such as Lausic created a kind of zero-sum calculus, if Lausic has responsibilities, Gotovina, Cermak, and Markac do not, is belied by HV regulations, for example, P880, articles 9 and 10, transcript 15214, belied by the jurisprudence which recognises the responsibility of superiors for the conduct of their subordinates, and is belied by common sense. As Lausic also noted, that is akin to the suggestion that parents who expect -- of parents who expect police to discipline their children. That's at P2159, paragraph 210. By then, it's far too late, even assuming that the police are interested or capable of doing that job. And the gap between the issuance of an order and the intention to see that it is meaningfully implemented is further illustrated by one of the orders cited by the Defence, Susak's prohibitions on the 2nd of August against "any kind of uncontrolled conduct." That's P409, page 3. As discussed in more detail in the Prosecution's final brief, at paragraphs 16, and 60 through 69, the reality of Susak's intentions regarding the implementation of those prohibitions is reflected in his reaction to the results of the systematic burning of Grahovo, declaring that Grahovo now being "ethnically clean" was one of the leadership's successes; by his ignoring of HV crimes, even when called upon to report about the situation in the liberated territory, see P2673, page 1; his active efforts to deny crimes to the international community, P598, pages 5 through 6; his role in devising strategies to keep Serbs from returning, P466, page 9; and his earlier involvement in psy-ops, intended to get civilians to flee while simultaneously providing a fig-leaf for Croatian authorities. The Prosecution's final brief also presents a detailed account of the measures undertaken by Croatian authorities in order to keep Serbs out after the vast majority had fled. Led by President Tudjman, the Croatian leadership instituted laws, under the "pretext" of preserving property - you will see that at P462, page 15 - during a discussion about those properties -- those measures with President Tudjman -- measures to effectively confiscate the property of those who did not reclaim it within an impossibly short deadline, also imposing bureaucratic obstacles to further ensure that the deadline could not be met. "The requirement that owners must reclaim their property by 27 December constitutes a virtually insurmountable obstacle for most Serb refugees." P650, page 9. Croatian authorities controlled this spigot of possible return and ensured that Serbs would not return in numbers that threatened the reversal of what had been achieved. And to further cement that demographic transformation, the Croatian leadership pursued a policy to resettle ethnic Croats, including persons from the diaspora, into formerly Serb areas. Now the Gotovina Defence has argued that Croatia was under no obligation to permit the return of Serbs who had opted to leave Croatia, and indeed, that Croatia was -- would have been within its rights to expel them, citing the Eritrea-Ethiopia Claims Commission Partial Award which the Trial Chamber has asked us to address. These arguments, Your Honours, ignore the very telling distinctions between that situation and this case. That award was based on findings that the expulsions were the result of a system applying a reasonable criteria to identify individuals thought to pose a threat, that is, individualised deportation through reasonable measures, and upon voluntary departure to reside on the territory of the enemy. Find those references at paragraph 72 and 73 of the decision. The award decision does not apply here. Individual determinations based on reasonable criteria are not analogous to forced deportation through shelling, burning or pillaging, and the award decision explicitly identifies that distinction at paragraph 89. Similarly, the accused are not charged for the voluntary departure of Serb civilians, so it is irrelevant that the -- a decision found that a country may be permitted to impose obstacles to return for those who left pursuant to a reasonable process or voluntarily. But the award decision, in another way, does remind us what the obstacles to return were about, where there seems no question that Ethiopia wanted these people out. The obstacles to return were intended to make permanent the departure of Serbs from the Krajina, not individual Serbs who posed a specific threat, but simply too many Serbs, whoever they were. As Tudjman said on the 30th of August: "If we let 204 come here, tomorrow you would have 1204, and in ten days 12.000. Nothing for now." As Sarinic said about Western Slavonia: "It was very positive for us, because no one came back." And, in that way, as another official told President Tudjman: "The Serb problem in Western Slavonia has been solved." Indeed, President Tudjman was so determined to cement the demographic transformation that he rejected proposals to return Croats who had been expelled from their homes in the Posavina because he feared that the same principle would be applied in Croatia, giving Serbs from Knin and Western Slavonia leverage to return to Croatia. As he said: "If we request for those 100.000 of Croats from Posavina to go back, then those 300.000 Serbs who left Croatia will request to come back as well." Even innocent Croats, like many innocent Serbs, were sacrificed to the vision of an ethnically homogeneous Croatia. In short, the ban or the obstacles to return were not about individualised concerns or bureaucratic difficulties, as Tudjman explicitly told Galbraith, Serbs could not be permitted to return. P445, paragraph 16. Or as he later told visiting dignitaries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, sometimes it's the interpreters who have difficulties to follow your speed of speech, sometimes it's the transcribers. Would you please make them at ease, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we see this contemporaneous cable on screen, Your Honour, which reflects: "Far from being apologetic, Tudjman yesterday told visiting congressmen that it would be impossible for these Serbs to return to the place where their families lived for centuries." President Tudjman was proud of what he had -- of what had been achieved and was not about to let it be undone. Look at his words on the one-year after anniversary of Storm: "The results that we have achieved are of historical importance. We have returned Zvonimir's Croatian town," that's Knin, "to the fold of its motherland Croatia, as pure as it was in Zvonimir's time." The accomplishment in which President Tudjman took such satisfaction, an ethnically pure Knin, was not his alone but was achieved by the acts and failures to act of a group, including the three accused, who implemented a common purpose to bring that about. Your Honours, I've nearly used up my allotted time. I wanted merely to quickly address one issue the Chamber raised in a question it had to the parties, and that's the issue of armed conflict, whether international or non-international. And in that respect, I wanted to note the following. First, the distinction between an international armed conflict and a non-international armed conflict is not relevant in this case. No Article 2 crime has been charged, so the Trial Chamber need not make that decision. It need only find that an armed conflict existed and in fact on that, the parties agree, with some dispute, as the Court is aware, about when it ended. However, should the Court be inclined to find from the evidence adduced or to characterise the conflict as international or non-international, we note the following. That per Tadic, a conflict is international, among other things, if another state intervenes in that conflict or if some participants act on its behalf. The record amply reveals the involvement of both factors. Indeed, the evidence is so extensive, I'll simply cite some categories. First is the direct involvement of outside forces, including the JNA and the HVO. Second is military operations outside the borders as part of the overall effort to subdue the Krajina Serbs. Third is the dependency of RSK political and military leaders on Serbian leaders. And the fourth I will mention is that a considerable part of the Defence was premised on the international aspect, including the need to finally defeat the RSK by going into Bosnia both before and after Storm, as well as the evidence detailed in paragraphs 44 through 49 of the Gotovina brief. And as for when the armed conflict ended, law is clear that the protections of international law apply from the beginning of an armed conflict beyond the cessation of general hostilities until a general conclusion of peace or a peaceful settlement is achieved. Once that conflict commences, fluctuations in intensity don't mean that the conflict is over. And the settlement of this conflict occurred with the Erdut Agreement in November and the Dayton agreement in December 1995, which ended the overall conflict. That's found at P451, pages xx and xxi. Your Honours, thank you for your attention. Mr. Russo will now address the Chamber concerning the unlawful shelling attack, forcible deportation -- or deportation and forcible transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Russo, once you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning to you good morning to Your Honours. I will be addressing the unlawful artillery attacks underlying the counts of persecution, forcible transfer and deportation which form part of the individual liability and JCE contributions of Generals Gotovina and Markac. I will begin by explaining how shelling caused the civilians to flee and then demonstrate the unlawfulness of that shelling. The Prosecution's case in a nutshell is that at the Brioni island meeting, a criminal plan was formed to force Serb civilians out of Croatia by targeting them with a combination of artillery strikes and psychological operations. That plan was successfully implemented during Operation Storm through shelling of Serb civilian population centres and the use of duplicitous leaflets and radio broadcasts telling Serb civilians to flee. The evidence could not be clearer or more consistent in showing that this is exactly what happened. All the arguments raised by the Defence are either irrelevant or contradicted by the totality of the evidence. And in some cases, both. For example, the Gotovina Defence argues that a pre-planned mass evacuation was the sole cause of civilian flight. This ignores the fact that the decision to evacuate civilians was made in response to the fact that civilians were already fleeing, in an unorganised manner, during the 11 hours preceding that decision. That can be found in the Prosecution's brief, paragraphs 637 to 642. The Milutinovic Chamber has recognised that the realities of war are not as simplistic as suggested by the Defence, and the fact that people may have left their homes for different reasons, even including instructions to leave, does not absolve an accused when their unlawful conduct was a primary cause of civilian flight. And that can be found in the Milutinovic Trial Judgement, volume 2, paragraphs 1175 and 76. But even if there was a pre-planned mass evacuation, which the facts do not support, it is irrelevant, because the civilian victims themselves testified to fleeing because of the unlawful shelling. The Defence ignored the witness evidence on this issue but the Chamber cannot because the only relevant question is what primarily caused the civilians themselves to flee. The civilian witnesses in this case, including Dopudj, Ilic, Torbica, and Witness P54, expressly stated that they fled because of the unlawful shelling. And that evidence can be found P548, paragraph 4; P726, page 2; P630, paragraph 4; and transcript page 2855. Other witnesses testified that they either fled as soon as possible after the shelling began or specifically mentioned shelling among the reasons why they fled. That evidence can be found in our brief at paragraphs 615 to 630. Contemporaneous reports of the HV and of international observers confirms that civilians began fleeing their towns and villages as soon as possible after the shelling began and, in any event, well before the decision to evacuate was even made. That evidence is at paragraphs 637 to 638 in our brief. The fact that so many of the civilian witnesses in this case had never heard of the evacuation decision, much less any plans for an organised and permanent departure from their ancestral homes in the Krajina, further demonstrates how immaterial the Defence's theory is to the ultimate issue before the Chamber. And that evidence is at paragraph 641 in our brief. Your Honours, I must ask to go briefly into private session for just a moment or two to discuss some of the evidence on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Jovan Dopudj observed people fleeing from Obrovac for the outlying villages as soon as the shelling started, and that the shelling soon spread to those outlying villages. That's P548, paragraphs 3 to 4. By 10.00 a.m., the shelling had spread to the villages around the roads, from Obrovac to Benkovac, namely, Krusevo, Bilisane and Zelengrad, as well as the villages on the road from Obrovac to Gracac. Namely, Zaton and Muskovci. That's also P548, paragraph 4. Here we see Mr. Dopudj's statement, P548, paragraph 8, where he recalled: "The way the attacks spread from the town of Obrovac to the other villages made it impossible to return at any point. It showed the goal of the operation was to cleanse the territory of Serbs, to expel them from there." This last comment cannot be dismissed as mere opinion because what the civilians themselves believed and felt as a direct result of the unlawful shelling of their towns is critical in determining the primary cause of their flight. The terrifying experience of having one's home attacked by artillery cannot be overstated or exaggerated, and the terrorising effect of an indiscriminate artillery attack is well established in the record. Witness after witness appeared before this Chamber to tell of watching their neighbours' houses and businesses being shelled. They attested to the hours of panic and uncertainty they and others suffered while cowering for shelter in basements or making a run for their lives on tractors to escape the shelling of their towns and villages. That evidence can be found in paragraphs 615 to 630 of our brief. Andries Dreyer, a UN security officer who led the effort to rescue civilians from the shelling in Knin, testified to finding them in states of extreme shock and panic, forcing him to slap some of them and to carry out others who could not be brought around. The natural and inevitable effect of such an attack on civilians was fear, panic and uncertainty, not only during those moments when they were in immediate danger from artillery, but also when considering their fate when the same Croatian soldiers who were attacking them with artillery arrived with guns in their hands. Vida Gacesa, a resident of Gracac who fled the shelling, summed it up perfectly in her statement. That's P119, paragraph 13: "The fact that we had been shelled all day and the fact that we were concerned that we would be alone in the village in the night and the panic that had been created amongst the people were the reasons that we decided to follow the others, even though we did not know where we were going to go." This and other evidence from the victims themselves admits of only one reasonable conclusion: That they fled to escape the widespread and unlawful artillery attacks on their towns and villages. I will now turn to the unlawfulness of the artillery attacks conducted by Generals Gotovina and Markac, in accordance with the common criminal plan. I will begin with the evidence that the JCE members planned and intended to conduct an unlawful attack on the Serb civilian population. I will then discuss how the method and means chosen for that attack demonstrate its unlawfulness and the intent behind it. I will end with the evidence showing that the attack was, in fact, directed at the civilian population. An unlawful attack is proven by: 1, an attack directed against the civilian population; or 2, an indiscriminate attack; or 3, a disproportionate attack. The Prosecution has presented evidence to establish all three types of unlawful attack beyond a reasonable doubt. But the Chamber need not consider the question of disproportionate attacks, as the evidence easily demonstrates that the artillery strikes ordered by Generals Gotovina and Markac were directed at the civilian population or were at least indiscriminate, in accordance with the common criminal plan formed at Brioni. In either case, the Prosecution has established the unlawfulness of the artillery attacks. The indiscriminate nature of the artillery attacks and the intent to drive out civilians is revealed through the statements of the accused and their co-conspirators, and also from the remarkable consistency between their statements and their actions, as documented in contemporaneous HV reports and corroborated by the percipient witnesses to the artillery attacks. The only reasonable explanation for that consistency is that the accused said what they meant and did what they said. As discussed earlier by Mr. Tieger, Tudjman put forward a plan at the Brioni meeting to seize the political opportunity to spark a mass flight of civilians by using a combination of psychological operations and unlawful artillery attacks. Generals Gotovina and Markac actively participated in that discussion and carried out their operations in accordance with it. And that's at P461, pages 10 through 15 for General Gotovina; and P461, pages 18 to 19 for General Markac, as an example. Mr. President, I'm about to go into an area which will cover several slides, and I see that we're approaching the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are approaching the break. If this would be a suitable moment, we'll take the break now, and we will then resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Gotovina Defence asks the Chamber to disregard the plain meaning of what Tudjman and others said at Brioni about getting the civilians out and to substitute an innocuous explanation which no witness substantiates and which is unreasonable, given the direct evidence of intent to force out civilians. The Defence would have the Court accept that all of these statements were simply recognitions that civilian flight would be a side effect of lawful military action. The Chamber must ask itself: Why would so much planning and discussion go into a mere side effect? President Tudjman tells us why at P461, page 15: "Because it was important that those civilians set out." His express indication of its importance meant that it was a definite objective not a possible side effect. No other reading is reasonable. Otherwise, why plan to drop leaflets telling Serb civilians to flee? Gojko Susak tells us why at P461, page 29. Because dropping leaflets "will provoke something." If civilian flight was just a side effect, why plan to broadcast the direction in which Serb civilians should flee? Dr. Miroslav Tudjman tells us why at P461, page 23: "So we have as little to do as possible." In his book, General Gotovina admitted to using leaflets directed at the civilian population. We see here in P1113, page 456, he even argued that they were successful: "If there had been no leaflets, they would have certainly stayed." The Gotovina Defence argues that General Gotovina is wrong about this, that leaflets were only used in Bosnia and that the Prosecution presented no witness who received a leaflet. But General Gotovina's account was confirmed by witness Marija Vecerina, who found one of the false ARSK leaflets on Mount Velebit and fled along the route indicated in the leaflet. That can be found at P652, paragraphs 7 through 10, and P653, paragraph 5. So it is clear that the Brioni plan to drive out civilians using psychological operations was successfully implemented. Let us now turn to the use of artillery. Tudjman's language at Brioni was clear and unambiguous. As we see from P461, page 10, he reminded everyone how many Croatian towns and villages had been destroyed, lamenting that Knin had not suffered the same fate. Tudjman was mindful of the political ramifications of completely destroying Knin with artillery which, by the way, General Gotovina, expressly offered to do. But Tudjman warned against doing anything in such an ill-conceived manner. And as we see at P461, page 11, he suggested instead that they give them just "a taste of it and we pay him back." This plan to use a measured dose of unlawful artillery strikes against the Serbs was in keeping with the plan to avoid international condemnation, but also with the effort to preserve the major civilian population centres from destruction so they could be swiftly repopulated with Croats, and you will hear more about that effort in Mr. Carrier's presentation. Tudjman made it clear that their planned use of artillery to get the Serb civilians out had to be disguised behind what could at least be argued as a legitimate use of artillery. P461, page 10, he says: "... their counter-attack from Knin and so forth, it would provide very good justification for this action, and, accordingly, we have the pretext to strike, if we can, with artillery ..." Your Honours, there is no misunderstanding or misinterpreting the word "pretext." The only reasonable explanation for needing a pretext was to disguise their true actions and motives for using artillery against civilian-populated areas. On 26 June 1995, approximately one month before the Brioni meaning, the HV Main Staff issued a directive regarding, among other things, the use of artillery in Operation Storm. That is Exhibit D956. The Defence concedes that General Gotovina's planning was to be governed by that directive, but they offer no discussion or explanation for why he deviated so significantly from it. Also absent is a discussion of the timing of that deviation, which happened immediately after the Brioni meeting. Here we see Exhibit D956, page 6, and the directive clearly indicates that artillery should focus on neutralising only two targets inside of Knin: One, the Main Staff which was in the ARSK HQ building; and, two, the 7th Corps Command, which, at the time was located in the northern barracks. In addition, it focuses on brigade command post, concentrations of enemy man power, et cetera, "in the area of Knin and Benkovac." But this directive is most important for what it does not say. It says nothing about using artillery against the civilian populations centres of Obrovac, Gracac, or Drvar. Immediately following the Brioni meeting, however, General Gotovina directed his chief of artillery, who was also present at that meeting, to begin selecting the targets for Operation Storm. That can be found in the Gotovina brief at paragraph 205. As we know from General Gotovina's attack order, the targets selected included whole towns that are not even included in this Main Staff directive. This proves that the original plan for the use of artillery was altered by General Gotovina as a result of the Brioni meeting, in order to make whole towns populated by Serbs the targets for artillery fire. In his attack order, which we see here, P1125, page 14, Gotovina explicitly directs his artillery to "put the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire." This order is not consistent with the Main Staff directive but is consistent with the Brioni plan to get civilians out because it unambiguously orders a direct attack on the Serb civilian population. Without any credible evidentiary support, the Gotovina Defence argue that everyone knew that this order actually meant to fire only against specific military targets within these towns. Nothing in the order itself, or in the way it was executed, supports that conclusion. There are no references to a tabular/textual attachment or to any other outside reference material clarifying any alleged targets inside of these towns. General Gotovina's order is detailed and specific in terms of what tasks were to be accomplished, by whom, when, and how. The precise detail with which he assigned all tasks in that order does not permit the Chamber to accept the Defence's unreasonable explanation, particularly in light of how of order was carried out. The Gotovina Defence also argue that the inclusion of Drvar in the order is somehow inconsistent with the Brioni plan to expel civilians from Croatian territory. General Gotovina answers this argument himself in his order appointing a commander in Drvar. That's D656, at page 1, where he explains that Drvar is "an area designated for the settling of displaced Croats." I refer the Court also to P447, page 1, a coded cable from Ambassador Galbraith to the Secretary of State, where he mentions the strategy to create a "Serb-free cordon sanitaire around the Croatian heartland ... by destroying Serb towns in western Bosnia." So the inclusion of Drvar, a town in western Bosnia, was entirely consistent with the Brioni plan to drive out Serbs and move in Croats. The Defence wrongly suggests that any evidence of HV artillery fire on ARSK front lines or other military objectives is somehow inconsistent with the Prosecution's position that Gotovina said precisely what he meant in his artillery order. But General Gotovina issued two separate orders in relation to use of artillery. We see again P1125, page 14. One order was to fire on military objectives, enemy front lines, command posts, et cetera; and the other, clearly separate order, directed the use of artillery against whole towns. Both orders were followed. Within the same reports, the HV simultaneously specify firing at whole towns and at specific targets within those towns and elsewhere. Just a few examples, P2533, page 3, where TS-4 reports "keeping Knin under fire." And also reporting firing at living buildings block in Knin, post office, police station, et cetera. P1200, page 2, the 134th Home Guard Regiment: "In the first few hours, we had no support from Zadar OG except for shelling of the general area of Benkovac without monitoring, and the message at 0530 hours of the following contents: Is anything falling on Benkovac?" P71, page 82, General Gotovina's own chief of artillery reporting to him: "Artillery attacks against enemy towns. Things were also done upon the requests of units." I'll refer the Chamber also to P1277, page 2, where OG Sibenik reports firing MBRLs "at Knin." P2436, page 6, where OG Zadar reports firing "at Gracac." This evidence is entirely consistent with the plain reading of General Gotovina's order and the Brioni plan to exploit a pretext for using artillery against civilians. General Gotovina's order was passed down almost verbatim, confirming a clear understanding of the plain language he used. His subordinates recognised that he meant what he said and understood that they were to pass on his order without further explanation or specification. We see the evidence of that here. General Gotovina's own chief of artillery: "Put the following towns -- put the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire." That's D970, page 3. One level below him, the OG Zadar commander: "Lay down fire on the towns of Benkovac and Obrovac." That's P1263, page 8. The OG Zadar chief of artillery: "Put the following towns under artillery fire: Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac." That's P1201, page 4. The plain meaning of General Gotovina's order is also borne out by the way in which it was executed. Both the method and the means of attack each violated the principle of distinction and reveal the intent to directly target civilians. As we have seen through General Gotovina's order and the contemporaneous reports of his troops, the method of his attack violated the principle of distinction because it treated entire civilian towns as targets. As the Milosevic Chamber recognised, the indiscriminate nature of an attack is strong indicia that it was, in fact, directed against the civilian population. That's the Milosevic Appeals Judgement, paragraph 66. As I demonstrated earlier, the decision to target whole towns and to deviate from the prior Main Staff directive was made at the Brioni meeting in accordance with the plan to force out civilians. Rajcic's report to General Gotovina that we just saw, indicating that the attack was against "enemy towns," reveals that the Serb civilian population was indeed considered the enemy and the target of attack. With regard to the means of attack, the weaponry chosen by General Gotovina was not capable of discriminating between military and civilian objects under the circumstances and therefore violated the principle of distinction. This is particularly true of the MBRLs, the air-burst artillery and the cluster munitions employed by General Gotovina against Knin. The evidence relating to that, Your Honours, can be found in our brief at paragraphs 594 to 613. The Gotovina Defence argument at paragraph 259 of their brief, that the principle of proportionality assumes that not all attacks will be able to hit only their intended objectives is not only wrong but fails to recognise that the principle of proportionality will only apply where the attack and the method and means of the attack is actually capable of distinguishing between military and civilian objects. Whether the weaponry used by General Gotovina complied with the principle of distinction is not a per se analysis, as suggested by the Defence, because Article 51(4) of Additional Protocol 1 makes clear that a case-by-case analysis is required for such a determination. The Chamber must determine whether General Gotovina's use of artillery and rockets in the particular circumstances of this case complied with the principle of distinction. In making that determination, the Chamber must consider that General Gotovina was firing at point targets in residential areas from 18 to 27 kilometres away, using weapons he knew would strike beyond those targets. That can be found in Rajcic's testimony, transcript page 16280 to 284. Under those circumstances, the weapons he chose were of a nature to strike both military and civilian objects without distinction, and that makes a proportionality analysis superfluous. In his book, General Gotovina only indicated that 130-millimetre cannons were used against Knin, significantly omitting his use of MBRLs. This telling omission reveals his awareness that his use of MBRLs in Knin could not be justified. Every witness with artillery knowledge in this case, including General Gotovina's own chief of artillery, testified that MBRLs are area weapons which are inappropriate for use against point targets in residential areas. That evidence is in our brief at 588 to 89. A perfect example of this is the ARSK HQ building, which the Defence claims to have been one of the primary targets of MBRL fire. Not one MBRL rocket out of the hundreds fired into Knin actually struck that building, despite the evidence that MBRLs were, in fact, fired at it. That can be found in Rajcic's evidence, P2339, section 3.2.1, transcript 16415 to 426. This demonstrates just how indiscriminate those weapons were under the circumstances. Given the inaccuracy and widespread use of MBRLs in Knin, MBRL rockets were landing in areas all over the town, including residential areas not close to any alleged military targets. That evidence is at paragraphs 595 to 601 in our brief. Although MBRLs were not capable of the necessary distinction under the circumstances, the evidence also shows that the HV deliberately targeted residential areas in Knin with MBRLs. One example is the 7th Guards Brigade's deliberate targeting of a residential area. The diary of the 7th Guards Brigade artillery commander shows that they fired MBRLs at targets labelled S-15, S-16, and S-54 on the Coded map entitled "Ivancica," which is Exhibit P2338. As a demonstrative aid to the Chamber, we have enlarged the relevant portion of the Ivancica map and have identified and highlighted the target circles S-15, S-16, and S-54. Just to orient the Chamber, the target S-15, which is the middle circle, is centred on the railway overpass bridge in the centre of down-town Knin. The target circle below that, which is S-54, is roughly centred on the ARSK HQ building, while S-16, which is the top circle, is centred on a residential area across the main road from the northern barracks. As a further demonstrative aid, we have overlaid these target circles on the aerial photograph of Knin, which is Exhibit P62, and have rotated that to correspond with the orientation of the Ivancica map. When considering the widespread effects of a rocket attack, it becomes clear that the 7th Guards Brigade basically blanketed down-town Knin with MBRL fire in clear violation of the principle of distinction. Even worse, however, is the direct targeting of S-16. As the Chamber will recall, that when this matter was put to Rajcic, he unsuccessfully tried to convince the Chamber that the 7th Guards Brigade actually fired on the northern barracks and not on the target S-16. That can be found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that the picture we see now on the e-court is so that we can normally read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We'll get to that --
