utterances.text: We've got it -- if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'll get to that in a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you turn it anti-clockwise, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, that's my next slide. Your Honours, even though the 7th Guards Brigade diary establishes that MBRLs were fired into the residential area, S-16, the Chamber also heard evidence of that fact from Captain Geoffrey Hill who testified to finding two exploded rocket bodies on the lawn of General Forand's house. What we have here is a further demonstrative showing that the target S-16, which was the top target on the previous slide, corresponds to the neighbourhood where Hill identified General Forand's residence on Exhibit P300. The two smaller red circles were places identified by Hill, and the one which appears within the overlay of target S-16 was the location where he found the rockets. Aside from the direct targeting of residential areas, the evidence also shows that MBRLs were fired into Knin at no particular targets during the night. The 7th Guards Brigade artillery commander's diary, P2455, records at page 21 that 40 MBRL rockets were fired "on Knin" at 40 minutes past midnight, between the 4th and 5th of August. That coincided with the time when Serb refugees were out in the open and being processed into the Sector South HQ. And that be found out P740, paragraph 2i; D284, page 12; and P748, page 6. At paragraphs 283 and 284 of their brief, the Gotovina Defence claims that these rockets were fired in the midst of alleged ARSK movements towards and through Knin. A close look at the evidence they cite, however, establishes that those movements were five to six hours after this volley of 40 rockets was fired into Knin. And that can be found specifically in the Gotovina brief, paragraph 284, footnote 492. The evidence of the percipient witnesses to the artillery attacks is fully consistent with the kind of indiscriminate attacks revealed by HV reports. In fact, not a single witness to the shelling gave an account even remotely consistent with the Defence's theory of a, quote/unquote, precise artillery strike on only high-value military targets. On the contrary, witnesses testified that shells fell all over their towns in no discernible pattern, and the damage to residential areas and the corresponding lack of damage to alleged military targets corroborates those accounts. That evidence can be found at paragraphs 525 to 537, and 544 to 560 of our brief. The Gotovina Defence's theory that the UN witnesses were all in collusion to falsely accuse Croatia of illegal shelling fails to account for the fact that the testimony of the UN witnesses is fully corroborated by and consistent with the testimony of all other international observers and also Serb civilians regarding the indiscriminate nature of the shelling. That evidence can be found in paragraphs 525 to 537 of our brief. In their brief, the Gotovina Defence did not discuss any evidence from the UNMO and Serb civilian witnesses regarding the shelling of Benkovac, Obrovac or Gracac. That testimony demonstrates the pattern of indiscriminate fire and the illegitimacy of the artillery attack as a whole. Now, Your Honours, my next set of slides are demonstratives regarding the towns identified in General Gotovina's order. And what I've done is overlaid on maps of these towns the alleged targets identified by the Gotovina Defence and by Rajcic, and also the areas where the witnesses identified shelling impacts. In the legend for each map, I have provided a citation to the evidence underlying the map, and I'm happy to provide copies of those demonstratives to the Chamber and to counsel as I will not be reading those citations into the record. Let's begin with Benkovac. Here we have the targets which the Gotovina Defence initially suggested were inside the town of Benkovac. These were based on maps prepared by the Gotovina Defence which cited no evidence indicating that the HV specifically fired at any of these alleged targets during Operation Storm. When General Gotovina's chief of artillery, Marko Rajcic, came to testify, the Defence did not put these targets to him, even though, according to his Defence statement, he selected the targets for the military operation and was "in charge of planning, coordinating, and controlling the use of artillery during Operation Storm." That can be found at D1425, paragraphs 1 and 5. Rajcic identified only one target actually inside the town of Benkovac itself and that's the middle target, which he identified as the police station. Now, the evidence established that there were no military targets in Benkovac on 4 August and that the police station was not a legitimate target for artillery fire. That evidence is set forth in paragraphs 570 to 572 of our brief. However, as with every other town named in General Gotovina's order, an argument about whether the targets identified by Rajcic were legitimate or not is unnecessary, once we consider the evidence of where the shells fired on Benkovac actually fell. We see those here in red. And these cannot be reasonably explained by a, quote/unquote, precise artillery strike against the only alleged target inside that town. Next is Obrovac. And we begin again with the targets which the Gotovina Defence initially claimed to have been in the town. Again, no evidence was provided to substantiate that the HV actually targeted these areas during Operation Storm, and, again, the Defence chose not to put these targets to Rajcic. He identified different targets. And taking a look at where the shells fell, we see again that they cannot be reasonably explained by reference to these alleged targets. Moving on to Gracac. We have the alleged targets initially identified by the Gotovina Defence. But Rajcic testified that with the exception of the cross-roads he circled: "There were no such military targets as could have been taken into consideration for firing with a view to possibly gaining a military advantage." That's transcript 16365. Zdravko Janic, a special police witness, testified that there were no military targets inside the town of Gracac proper. That's transcript 16 -- I'm sorry, 6393 to 94. Nevertheless, we see shells were indeed fired into Gracac proper and not only in the vicinity of the cross-roads. Before moving on to Knin, I would like to address General Markac's JCE contribution and separate individual liability for the planning and ordering of the illegal special police artillery attack on Gracac. Now, with regard to the shelling of the town, the evidence does not distinguish which of the areas depicted here in red are attributable just to General Markac versus General Gotovina, but the distinction, Your Honours, is irrelevant, not only because of their JCE participation but because they both ordered firing into Gracac. And that evidence is in our brief at paragraph 413. And the lack of military targets inside the town made any firing into Gracac unlawful. As argued in our final brief, General Markac bears responsibility for all crimes charged in the indictment, including the unlawful artillery attacks on all towns, given his participation in the JCE, but I will focus here only on his liability for planning and organising the attack on Gracac. General Markac participated in the Brioni meeting. The town of Gracac was in his area of responsibility and he participated in the planning and ordering of the attack on that town consistent with the criminal plan formed at Brioni. For purposes of Operation Storm, the special police forces were subordinated to the Main Staff, and General Markac was directed by the Main Staff to coordinate his attack with General Gotovina, which he did. That evidence can be found, P1150, pages 37 to 38; P554, page 1; D543, page 2; D1094, page 2; and D1425, paragraph 57. General Markac also issued the special police attack order for Storm which included the special police artillery attack. And that's P614, page 6. Despite there being no military targets inside the town of Gracac itself, the town was shelled on both the orders of Gotovina and Markac. Rajcic attempted to isolate himself and General Gotovina from the shelling of Gracac by testifying that the 130-millimetre guns of TRS-5, which had Gracac in range, were resubordinated to General Markac's special police forces. And that's in the Gotovina brief, paragraph 228. However, the evidence demonstrates that the 130-millimetre guns which were used to fire on Gracac remained under the command of Gotovina and simply provided support to General Markac on his axis of attack. In his analysis of Operation Storm, General Gotovina later recalled that this is exactly how it happened when he wrote that he ordered the TRS-5 to "provide a constant and uninterrupted support to the forces on my left wing and on their right flank." Referring to the special police forces. That's P1192, page 3. Josip Turkalj, General Markac's chief of artillery, also testified that for firing on Gracac, he only received support from the guns belonging to the Croatian army, not that they were resubordinated to the special police. That's at transcript pages 13599 to 600. The fact that Gracac was shelled under both General Gotovina's and General Markac's orders is proven by the contemporaneous HV and special police reports which show that the first special police request for artillery fire "on Gracac" did not come until 9.00 a.m. on 4 August. But consistent with all other towns shelled by General Gotovina, the shelling of Gracac began at 5.00 a.m., and only General Gotovina's 130-millimetre guns had Gracac in range at that time. That evidence is P2385, page 2; P2436, page 6; P516, paragraph 20; and P553, page 59; and D971. Now on to Knin. Though the scale of shelling in Knin dwarfs that of the other towns, the pattern remains the same. We begin with the alleged targets initially identified by the Gotovina Defence. These 29 alleged targets were not put to Rajcic either in his Defence statement or during his testimony, despite the fact that he personally oversaw the shelling of Knin. Rajcic himself identified only the following 11 targets. The Defence have not discussed the obvious discrepancy between their version of events and that of Gotovina's own chief of artillery. Nevertheless, the question of whether the alleged targets identified by Rajcic were legitimately attacked with artillery is superfluous, in light of where the shells actually landed in Knin. Your Honours, no amount of military jargon about the centre of gravity, or full-spectrum operational dominance, or air/land battle, or the manoeuvrist approach, or any other military doctrine justifies the wild discrepancies between the alleged targets of attack and the actual evidence of what was shelled in Knin. Looking at the cumulative evidence of the percipient witnesses to the artillery attack on Knin, it is a small wonder that they uniformly report that shells were falling all over the town. Indeed, it is just as Andries Dryer observed when he was asked to circle on this photo the areas where he saw shells land. He said: "What I should have done is I should have taken a big pen and drawn a circle right around Knin and not specify and say, This is the area of impact, because that was the area of impact. Knin itself, in all directions where I travelled." That is transcript page 1740 to 41. The HV fired a minimum of 1.000 shells into Knin over the course of a 25-hour artillery campaign. That evidence is detailed at paragraph 544 of our brief in footnote 1993. But only a handful of those 1.000 shells actually struck any of the alleged targets. Rajcic identified only three "main and highest payoff targets" for the attack, which were the ARSK HQ, the northern barracks, and the post office. Than's at D1425, paragraph 15. The number of artillery strikes these alleged targets received after 25 hours of attack belies the, quote/unquote, precise shelling argued by the Defence. The ARSK HQ, the alleged highest-value target, according to Rajcic, received one shell hit. And that one shell landed in the parking lot. Than's transcript page 18465, Witness AG58; and P1094, paragraph 41, Witness Novakovic. The evidence also showed that civilians actually ran into this building during the artillery attack, which is hardly a situation that can be envisioned were it the obvious object of a precise and concentrated artillery attack. And that evidence is at P1094, page -- paragraph 19. The post office received no shell hits and no damage. No witness who testified about damage from artillery in down-town Knin mentioned any damage to the post office. And D389, the ARSK report on shelling damage early on 4 August does not mention any damage or strikes on the post office. The northern barracks received an unknown but completely negligible number of artillery strikes, given that it showed no visible damage and that the HV moved right in and started using it on 5 August. That is P292, page 100; P429, paragraph 32; P84, page 2; P980, page 4. Here again, the evidence showed civilians running into this complex. That is P71, page 84. The Chamber will recall that the northern barracks is a very large facility encompassing approximately 150.000 square metres and could unquestionably have been much more precisely targeted with the 130-millimetre guns used by General Gotovina. Even looking beyond the alleged highest-value targets, we see that the same pattern generally holds, few hits and negligible damage to all of the remaining targets with the sole exception of the Tvik factory. That evidence is in our brief at paragraphs 550 to 563.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if would you allow me one question so that I'm better able to follow your argument. In respect of the ARSK headquarters and the northern barracks, you say -- I didn't hear you say that these are not considered to be military targets. You said, But the civilians fled into that complex or in that building. Wise or unwise, but that's what they did. I mean, if I were a civilian, I don't know whether I would seek refuge in a complex or a building which could be considered to be a military target. That's at least -- some risks involved. But I do not fully understand what you mean exactly when you say, Well, even if it is a military target, civilians fled into that building or that complex. Is that that they would -- well, just don't fully understand what the reasoning is you're applying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me first clarify that I'm not attempting to indicate that the fact that civilians ran in somehow changes the military character of that particular building. The reason I'm pointing out that evidence is an indication that the ARSK HQ and the northern barracks were not actually, as suggested by the Defence, the focus of this artillery attack. In other words, if they had been precisely and concentratedly shelled as suggested, then perhaps the civilians would not have run towards those buildings in order to get in them. That's the only point I'm making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I understand you well, you say that the fact that they were hit or seen to have been targeted only so little by civilians would have caused them to overcome any doubt as to whether you could go there or not. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The extremely low number of artillery strikes on the alleged targets compared to the number of shells fired into the town cannot be reasonably explained. The Defence's argument that the HV was only trying to harass, suppress or neutralise these alleged targets is nonsense. How is this pattern of shelling, which we see here, reasonably possible if General Gotovina conducted a, quote/unquote, precise and, quote/unquote, judicious artillery attack with appropriately discriminate weapon. It is not possible. The only reasonable conclusion is that, consistent with his explicit order, General Gotovina directly targeted the civilian population of Knin and other civilian towns in the Krajina, causing almost the entire Serb civilian population to flee for their lives. In the aftermath of this unlawful attack, those few Serbs who could not or would not flee their homes would soon face the wave of burnings, lootings, killings, and harassment at the hands of Croatian forces, and I will leave it to Mr. Hedaraly to address those crimes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Mr. Hedaraly, I will also ask your attention for all those who have to transcribe or translate your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The end of the artillery attack was a beginning of a nightmare for Serb civilians, mostly infirm and elderly, who remained in their homes. They were harassed, intimidated, many killed. They saw members of the Croatian forces plunder their property and destroy their houses. The destruction was widespread and in many, if not most cases, Croatian forces looted the houses before burning them. As referenced in paragraph 646 of the Prosecution's final trial brief, ECMM reported in late August 1995 that 60 to 80 per cent of houses had been destroyed; UNMO reported 73 per cent on 13 September; and other internationals placed the figure closer to 80 to 90 per cent of the villages having suffered some form of burning. International witnesses and reports regularly made statements such as: "The majority of the sector was on fire." And, "The Krajina is burning." As an example, Mr. Vanderostyne testified that the burning was on a large scale and was asked to clarify for this Chamber what he meant by a large scale, he told this Trial Chamber - it's on the screen - that from a small hill between Gospic and Gracac, he could see the entire country side burning "everywhere, every farm, every barn, every annex, every house in the countryside." As the Chamber can see from Annex A of the Prosecution's final brief, this destruction started as soon as HV forces entered the former RSK-controlled territory on 5 August 1995, with Serb houses seen burning on that day in the municipalities of Knin, Benkovac, Kistanje, Orlic, and Ervenik. HV reports themselves confirmed that significant amount of destruction took place almost immediately following the arrival of Croatian soldiers. On 13 August, Colonel Zelic writes that: "The largest number of fires occurred a day or two following the entry of HV units into newly liberated villages." And that the arson was "most often carried out by members of Home Guards Regiments." These Croatian forces which entered the area on 5 August also engaged in extensive looting. For example, the Prosecution has referred in its final brief, at paragraph 659, about looted goods being collected outside the UN camp. International witnesses, upon being able to go into Knin, noted that "each and every single house was broken into" and looted. Although the Gotovina Defence suggested at paragraph 414 of its brief that these were "security sweeps" in Knin, at least one witness, Erik Hendriks, when asked specifically at transcript reference 9823 whether what he saw in Knin on 7 August was consistent with such searches said that it was not. Croatian forces were continuing to plunder Serb property and destroy Serb houses. In the words of the UN political and humanity coordinator for Sector South, Hussein Al-Alfi, it was "a daily ritual." The HV operational diary for the Split Military District, P71, itself noted the problem of looting and burning. 11 August: "Everything is looted. The looting is the problem." 14 August: "Complaints against burning of village Benkovac where there are no Chetniks." 19 August: "Burning is a huge problem. Journalists and others could prove that it was arson." On 14 August 1995, ECMM reported that the systematic destruction and burning of large areas was continuing, with houses burnt in practically every town. On 20 August, UNCIVPOL reported a callous trend of widespread arson, involving Croatian military personnel spotted at the scene. On 22 August, Eric Hendriks observed this house in Guglete, P948, burning, with two uniformed military police HV members with 72nd Battalion insignia, together with three civilians and the support of a INA light truck leaving the scene. D820, page 5; and P938. On 24 August, the Knin police administration responded to Assistant Minister Moric and stated that HV members with military vehicles were driving away stolen property. On 31 August, UNCRO reports that the "burning of houses continues in a steady and methodical manner ... and that it is difficult to believe that these atrocities -- these activities are occurring without at least the tacit approval of the authorities." Your Honours, in addition to the reports of the international observers, almost every single Serb civilian who stayed in his or her village and who provided evidence to this Chamber described soldiers entering their villages and either burning, looting, or both. Bogdan Brkic in Palanka; Petar Colovic in Orlic; Vesela Damjanic in Biskupija; Bogdan Dobric in Dobropoljci; Konstantin Drca in Parcici; Milica Djuric in Djurici; Jovan Grubor in Grubori; Rajko Gusa in Bukovic; Milan Ilic, Orahovac; Milica Karanovic in Grubori; Petar Knezevic, Oton Polje; Milan Letunica in Gosic; Smiljana Mirkovic, Polaca; Mirko Ognjenovic, Kakanj; Jovan Popovic in Mokro Polje; Manda Rodic, Strmica; Draginja Urukalo, Biskupija; Jovan Vujnovic, Oton Polje; Stevan Zaric, Orlic; Junjga Dragutin, Uzdolje; as well as witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I see we have a problem with the transcript. It has stopped after the first name you started mentioning and many followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Are these only the individual screens, Your Honour, or is it the -- I don't have access to the main --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think it's also my ... well, it seems that now the -- our transcriber has apparently put all the names in but it did not appear on our screens. The matter seems to be resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honours, those are no less than 22 names who provided evidence to this Chamber. And with the exception of the witnesses who discussed Grubori, the incidents referred by these witnesses took place between the 5th and the 11th of August. As indicated in Annex A of the Prosecution's final brief, the burning and looting continued throughout the months of August and September, with reports of Croatian soldiers looting in late September and also seen in the immediate vicinity of burning houses. To add to the reports from internationals and testimony from local Serb civilians, Pero Perkovic, a soldier in the 15th Home Guard Regiment, testified how he rode on a truck that contained television sets and other goods that had been looted from the Serb houses in Kistanje on the 6th or 7th of August. That can be found at transcript reference 19534, 35, 38, as well as 45 and 46. Mr. Perkovic's testimony was also indicative of the general climate of impunity that reigned in the area. All a commander did when he saw the truck was to shout at the soldiers by asking them what kind of soldiers they were to be looting. That truck was never stopped and went through two or three check-points manned by the civilian and the military police. International witnesses, such as Mr. Marker Hansen, testified that it was a regular occurrence for him and his ECMM patrol to be stopped at check-points while military vehicles loaded with looted goods would get through. Transcript 14927. One of the few soldiers ... one of the few soldiers who was convicted for these acts, in this case for looting in the Kosovo valley on 2 September, provided a glimpse into the attitude that prevailed among Croatian forces at the time. A member of the 113th Brigade, his defence before the military court, was that since everyone was looting, why not him? That's at P2609, page 5. Some of the soldiers carrying out these crimes did not seem to care that they were observed looting goods and burning houses in public, with the presence of internationals not disturbing them and without trying to hide what they were doing. In other cases, the Croatian soldiers carrying out these crimes threatened international observers. For example, Mr. Flynn, at P20, page 26, about soldiers threatening an HRAT team who wished to inspect one of the houses they could see burning; or Mr. Berikoff, transcript 7706, who said he was threatened and soldiers tried to take his camera; and at transcript 8325 and 8569, ECMM monitors observing Croatian soldiers burning houses along the Knin-Drnis road had shots fired above their head. The destruction was targeted predominantly against Serbs. As noted in paragraph 646 of the Prosecution's final brief and its accompanying footnotes, the mainly Serb towns of Kistanje, Djevrske, Cetina, Donji Lapac, were more than 95 per cent destroyed, with Donji Lapac, 99 per cent Serb before the war, described by Minister Susak as nothing more than a name on a map. P470, page 53. By contrast, the villages of Podlapac, Siveric and Bruska, which according to international observers were mainly Croat, were spared from destruction. Spared also were the larger towns so that they could be repopulated with Croat displaced persons. Spared also were houses that had been marked as being Croat so that they would not be destroyed or looted further. For example, one witness who also stated how he believed the looting and the burning was organised, also stated how only Serb houses were burned in villages where the population was mixed; P487, paragraph 74. The Prosecution also included in its final brief evidence relating to churches having been preserved and in some cases being guarded and not destroyed. This is footnote 2333 of the Prosecution's brief, indicating a level of organisation belying random acts of isolated individuals. Witnesses often indicated that these crimes were committed by Croatian soldiers, identifying them because of their uniform. The Prosecution does not deny that civilians were involved in the commission of crimes, and particularly looting as time went on, but most of these crimes were committed by soldiers or by civilians in concert with soldiers, and there are examples in our brief. Even when witnesses did not identify a specific unit, there is ample evidence showing that the HV had virtual complete control of the territory when it entered on 5 August. Most internationals were not allowed to leave the UN camp before the 7th of August, and patrol outside Knin even later. Check-points were established to prevent civilians from entering the area, and the first significant arrival of Croat displaced persons was on the 15th of August, when passes were no longer necessary. Further references can be found at paragraph 479 of the Prosecution's brief. But as the UN CIVPOL report for 20 August that I referred to earlier stated, there was hardly anyone else in the area to blame. Some witnesses did specifically identify units. For example, at P2395, one witness specifically named the 4th Guards Brigade and the Pumas, and gave an example of ten military trucks of the 7th Guards Brigade and ten military trucks carrying looted goods. That's page 5, 6, and 7 of P2395. In the face of all of this evidence about systematic, organised and open destruction and plunder, the Gotovina Defence has chosen to focus its attention on the flaws that it found with P176, the UNMO assessment of damage. The Chamber will recall that the UNMOs found that of 22.213 buildings, 8.063 were totally damaged and 9.207 partially damaged. The Prosecution is not claiming that the UNMO survey represents a perfect and flawless account of the destruction but, rather, only one of many sources of evidence indicating the widespread nature of the destruction. Recognising that there were some discrepancies in the totals, the Prosecution did the following, and simply for demonstrative and illustrative purposes, we removed the villages that were duplicated, removed entries where there were blank entries for the total number of houses and removed the entries where the survey itself noted pre-Storm damage and we have re-totalled the columns. There were also other issues raised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. With all due respect, and I do apologise to my colleague, there is simply no basis for this, nothing whatsoever, coming in and recalculating this, and offer as if it's now a gospel truth. And I do -- I'm hesitant to object because I know that the Chamber is not in favour of that. But I do feel quite strongly about this document that it's completely of no basis whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Prosecution develop its argument. Gospel truth is not, at this moment, immediately decided whether it exists or not. The apparently new calculations have been made by the Prosecution. We'll see to what extent that does in any way remedy the flaws that were indicated and whether it's complete or not. At the same time, Mr. Hedaraly will be aware that just giving one screen, not knowing exactly what was considered to be duplicate, what was -- I mean, what's the basis for the new calculations, that, of course, the Chamber, in order to verify the accuracy of it, that it might need more information and just the pink colour on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just for the record, Mr. President, on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, we simply have no way to verify the accuracy or to investigate this at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I was clear enough that you would need more information to verify the accuracy, and we leave it to Mr. Hedaraly whether he comes back to it. He might also wait and see what the Defence teams in their final arguments will raise in respect of this and then use the time remaining to give further explanation. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I apologise to Mr. Hedaraly, but we will join in that objection, Your Honour. And in addition, obviously leaves us no opportunity to cross-examine anything relating to this document since this underlying survey was the subject of intense cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What apparently the Prosecution has done is to -- it has reviewed some of the evidence and has developed some thoughts on it, in view of what was argued by the various Defence teams as being flawed, and I think they're entitled to do so. If they do not give sufficient explanation, it is not only the Defence but also the Chamber which will not be able to verify that. So let's see what comes and let's -- let's allow the Prosecution to develop its thoughts. Mr. Hedaraly, anything -- I briefly responded to the observations made by Mr. Kehoe and by Mr. Kuzmanovic. If you want to add something, that's fine. If you consider that the Chamber has understood what you are doing at this moment, and if you have also understood that presenting new numbers as apparently the result of a new calculation, that it's difficult to verify with not knowing exactly what the basis for that new calculation is. That if you have understood that well, and if you will address that matter now or at any later stage, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Of course, in the -- and this is simply meant to show that the factors that I have raised, some of them which were raised by the Defence, simply those factors that I have already listed just to illustrate the difference was not as significant. This is not evidence that I'm tendering or these numbers are not submitted as evidence. But the Chamber has understood the purpose of what I was trying to achieve. There were also other issues raised regarding the survey, such as discrepancies with the 1991 census, the methodology as to how the numbers were obtained, and whether all the teams reported pre-Storm damage. I will not address all of these but simply point out, Your Honours, that there is evidence in the record regarding these issues. Sometimes -- for example, the evidence of Mr. Puhovski, at 16121, regarding the census numbers; the evidence of Mr. Marti and Mr. Tchernetsky, saying that they did, in fact, record pre-Storm damage, at 4705 and 3225. And even though this survey that the UNMOs conducted may not be a perfect account of each and every single house or structure that was destroyed after the 5th of August, in fact, you will note if you examine the survey, that neither Kistanje nor Djevrska, where the destruction is well documented, are included in P176. The more important point, Your Honour, is the following. What the UNMO survey does is confirm and corroborate all the other evidence I have recited to you in these last few minutes. The evidence of other internationals who stated that at almost every village houses were destroyed, the figures of 60 per cent destruction rising up to 90 in rural areas mentioned by others, and the evidence of almost all the Serb civilians who stayed in their homes and who provided evidence to this Chamber. One last note on the destruction, the Gotovina Defence cites to Mr. Flynn and his estimate of at least 500 houses being destroyed about three weeks after Operation Storm. Mr. Flynn himself, several times, at transcript reference 1314 to 18, stated that it was probably a very conservative estimate. It is an indeed an extremely low figure at odds with the weight of the evidence but I also remind the Chamber that Mr. Flynn also testified that the burning was a result of a systematic campaign. P21, paragraph 11. And when asked to explain, he stated that it was the scale of the burning and the large number of fires that principally led him to this conclusion. The effect of all of this, Your Honours, as one international organisation has noted, was that the burning of the Krajina Serb farming resources effectively prevents them to return in large numbers; P2150. Indeed, when one witness was asked why after seven weeks in the UN camp she went to Serbia rather than return to her home, she answered at transcript 16652, and I quote: "How could we possibly go back home if our home had been burned down? We had no home to go back to." Your Honour, I note the time. I will be moving in a different area, so this may be a suitable time for an earlier break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Hedaraly. We'll have a break and we will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The criminality in the Krajina after 4 August extended beyond plundering and destroying Serb property and included the killing of hundreds of Serb civilians. These killings also started as soon as the Croatian forces entered the area, with most occurring in the first several days after 5 August. The murders charged by the Prosecution were all against civilians, including women and elderly, and they were often killed by gun-shots. When looking at the evidence in its totality and also considering the considerable evidence regarding killings, both from the witnesses who testified in court and those who provided evidence under Rules 92 bis and 92 quater, a certain pattern does emerge. Before going into specific incidents, I want to discuss three general factors that make this pattern apparent and refutes claims that these killings were random. First, the date of the killings; second, the age and sex of the victims; and third, the cause of death. With respect to the date of the killings, the Prosecution has reviewed all its evidence in Appendix B, which is additional killings and its scheduled killings, and has come to the following conclusion. Before showing you my next slide, though, there was one methodological point that I want to make. In cases where there was no specific date of death because the only evidence was that the body was collected, the Prosecution, relying on the evidence that the later the body was collected the more decomposed it used to be, has considered the following dates of death. If the body was collected the 15th of -- before the 15th of August, it considered that the death has -- had occurred the day before. If -- if the body was collected before the 31st of August, it considered that death had occurred three days before. And if the body was collected in the month of September, it considered that it was five days before. Once again, this is simply for illustrative purposes and is underlied by the evidence in the Prosecution's final brief. So when we look at this evidence on the date of the killings, we can see that the 182 of the 324 victims, both scheduled and from the further clarification killings, occurred before the 10th of August. That's the figure in the red on your screen. And if we include the figure in orange, the killings that occurred before the 15th of August, where, once again, there is significant evidence that the area was under exclusive control of Croatian forces, the proportion reaches over two-thirds. In terms of victims, all 324 victims were either civilians or soldiers hors de combat. But within that group, we can see that 97 were women, that 55 of these women were over the age of 60; 87 of the victims were men over the age of 60. When we put that in a graphic form, we see that 184 of the 324 victims were women, including elderly ones, and elderly -- elderly men. Just -- just for the Court's reference, the term "others" does not only include men who were 60 or younger but also those men for whom a specific date of birth was not available. Now while all the victims were civilians or hors de combat, this large proportion of women and elderly victims suggests that anyone remaining in the Krajina was a target. In terms of cause of death, the Chamber knows that there are not autopsy reports for all the victims, most often in the case of bodies that were not buried in the Knin or Gracac cemeteries from where the Prosecution carried out its exhumations. Therefore, the evidence must be examined in its totality, including, for example, the presence of visible injuries at the time the body was collected or accounts that the body had been burnt. In some cases, despite the presence of an autopsy report, the cause of death is unascertained. An unascertained cause of death does not necessarily exclude a violent death and the Chamber has already noted, in an exchange with Dr. Clark, at transcript reference 14251, that the evidence must be - and I'm paraphrasing, obviously - that other factors must also be considered. In some case, the cause of death is unascertained because of the advanced state of decomposition of the body and the fact that the forensic examination took place years after the death, or, in some cases, in the case of Nikica Panic, victim number 124, his head was missing and a forensic examination could therefore not determine a specific cause of death. Once again, the evidence must be addressed in its totality, including evidence of internationals and locals who saw the body, as well as evidence that the Chamber has received regarding the murders and violence committed against the Serb civilians. What we do find in those autopsy reports, however, is the following. 81 of the 324 victims - that's the portion in red - listed by the Prosecution, died from at least one gun-shot injury to the head. Another 96 from gun-shots to other parts of their body for a total of 177, more than half. That's in the orange. If we look at the yellow, at the bottom, this is a category called "Possible Gun-shots" which is simply when the autopsy report specifically included a gun-shot as a likely cause of death. So, for example, if it said "blast injury" or "gun-shot," those are classified as possible gun-shots. Any claim that these killings by gun-shots were result of combat is rendered even more unreasonable if we look at the data for women and -- and elderly men. And once again the data underlying all these charts is found in the evidence regarding each of these killings. We can see that more than half the elderly men, the blue and the darker purple at the top, were killed by gun-shots. And if we add the possible gun-shots, the proportion reaches over 70 per cent. With the women as well, more than half were killed by gun-shots. I also take this opportunity to note one of these women that was killed by gun-shot to the head was Ilinka Crnogorac, which is victim number 156. In their brief, the Gotovina Defence referred to the Knin police log-book in support of the proposition that she had died of natural causes. The Gotovina Defence lists victim number 314 but the name that appears on the document is this victim, but that -- be that as it may. The Knin police log-book entry states that the victim had died of natural causes. The Croatian police told the same thing to ECMM monitors, that's recorded at P2157, telling them that the 67-year-old woman had died of low blood pressure, even though the monitors found blood and a bullet casing in the house of the victim and were told by other locals that the woman was killed by HV soldiers. The autopsy report, which will come up on your screen, confirms the account of the locals and internationals as it shows that she, in fact, died from a close-range gun-shot wound to the head. There is another similar example also cited in the Gotovina final brief from victim number 127, where the Knin log-book at page 70, state that she died of natural causes, but where Dr. Clark testified that she likely died of a gun-shot injury. The references are in footnote 660 of Appendix B of the Prosecution's final brief. As I alluded to earlier, assessing this evidence in its totality also means considering it in light of the detailed evidence you have received about other killings. You saw the statistical evidence showing that most killings occurred before 10 August and that two thirds occurred before the 15th of August. You also heard testimonial evidence that Croatian forces started killing civilians as soon as they entered the territory. For example, scheduled killings number 2, 3, 7, and 10, all occurred between the 5th and the 7th of August. You have also received significant evidence regarding other killings from witnesses who provided evidence under Rules 92 bis and 92 quater. These witnesses describe, sometimes in detail, the circumstances of the murder of their family members and neighbours. With respect to some specific murders, the Gotovina Defence has presented a number of arguments, and in many cases its interpretation of what happened, or, rather, in many cases, what may have happened, often based on unreasonable and implausible conclusions. I will not have time to address all of these today but simply a few examples to show the Chamber why they should exercise strong caution when assessing these arguments and carefully analyse all the evidence before drawing its inferences. At the outset, for example, you are told about alleged duplications. For example, that victims 48 and 79 are likely duplicates. They are not. The bodies were recovered in different locations between 3 and 5 kilometres apart, and witnesses who recovered one of the bodies noted bullet wounds on the legs which the autopsy report of the other victim did not. This can be found in footnotes 374 and 493 of Appendix B. Similarly, it is suggested that victims 305 and 306 are the same, although you heard from the ECMM witness who found the bodies, Eric Hendriks, who testified to having seen two bodies and also saw photographs depicting two bodies. This evidence is found at footnotes 984 and 985 of Appendix B. I have already discussed two of the examples given for death by natural causes. Let me go into a little more detail about one particular example, the killing of Jovica Plavsa, with respect to which the Chamber has received a significant amount of evidence in the litigation surrounding the admission into evidence of the statement of his father, Nikola Plavsa. The evidence from Nikola Plavsa is that his son was taken away in handcuffs by Croatian soldiers on the 5th of August, that he heard a shot from the direction where his son was taken, and found the body of his son some 10, 15 minutes later. P2686. This account is corroborated by the autopsy report, which found a set of handcuffs looped in the right radial bone. After having argued the litigation surrounding the admission into evidence of the statement that Jovica Plavsa had died during combat, the Gotovina Defence is now attempting to convince you - paragraphs 262 to 264 - that the victim was shot while the military police was trying to handcuff him, as regular soldiers apparently don't carry handcuffs, because handcuffs were found looped around one bone of the victim's arm. Your Honour, this farfetched conclusion proposed by the Defence is not plausible, is not reasonable and, crucially, is not supported by the evidence. The only reasonable conclusion is that the victim was taken away in handcuffs, as stated by the victim's father, and executed by the 4th Guards Brigade soldiers in Golubic whose presence there on that day is not disputed. Let me quickly mention one more example, the murder of Jovanka Mizdrak. That's number 180. Here, a witness testified that two HV soldiers left the convoy. One of them shot at her house, destroying all the windows. When the victim refused to leave her house, she was shot by an HV soldier. That is at P637. Pointing to an UNMO report, P229, where apparently this witness told UNMOs that the HV soldier asked the women to surrender and that the victim refused and ran into her house, the soldier shot her in the back. Leaving aside why an HV soldier would ask two women to surrender on 8th August, according to the Defence, it was not unreasonable for an HV soldier to shoot a 50-year-old woman in the back, whose only fault seems to have been to be scared by the presence of armed HV soldiers apparently asking her to surrender. With respect to the scheduled killings, Your Honour, the Prosecution is mindful of the Chamber's guidance and will therefore not repeat the arguments contained in our final brief, just make one general comment which extends beyond the killings, that is the cases where the credibility of the Prosecution witnesses were put into question and, particularly, its so-called crime-base witnesses. The Chamber is aware of the difficult task facing these witnesses, often elderly, who are forced to relive traumatic circumstances. The Chamber has observed their testimony and their demeanour and, from the Prosecution's view, the truthful accounts of what they have witnessed. This is an example. You will recall the difficult questions that Milica Djurica had to answer regarding why she didn't say anything about smelling her husband's burning flesh, how it was suggested that she was lying about having to bury her husband's remains and so on. And you heard her responses. You can find one of these at transcript reference 10821. Quickly, in passing, on scheduled killing number 7, the Gotovina Defence only addressed the evidence of Witness P3, did not address the very powerful, very important and very compelling evidence of other witnesses, including Witness P67. The reference is in our final brief. Finally, one very quick word on Counts 8 and 9. The Prosecution simply notes that the Gotovina Defence, on a few instances, particularly when discussing the case of Draginja Urukalo, the Chamber will recall was a 70-year-old woman who was forced by an HV soldier to strip to her underwear and play basketball, that she was physically unharmed by a one-time event of limited duration and that therefore did not qualify as a violation under Counts 8 and 9. Now whether the Gotovina Defence considers that forcing a 70-year-old woman to undress in such a way and play basketball is inhumane or not, the law is clear. In the recent Haradinaj case, the Appeals Chamber last month found, in paragraphs 95 and 96, that mental suffering which constituted a serious attack on human dignity constituted cruel treatment. Applying this law to the facts in the case of Ms. Urukalo, the only reasonable inference to be drawn is that the HV soldiers who forced her to strip and play basketball committed cruel treatment. Your Honours, what I have cited today in terms of murder, cruel treatment, destruction, and plunder are only examples of what took place in the Krajina after the 5th of August. The extent, scale, and regularity of these crimes are well-documented and the testimony of the numerous witnesses, including those with victims who suffered the most from these crimes, can lead to only one reasonable conclusion. They were primarily carried out by Croatian forces against Serb civilians and Serb property. Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you for carefully listening to these submissions. Ms. Gustafson will now address the criminal liability of General Gotovina for these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Ms. Gustafson, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good afternoon and thank you. Your Honours, you have heard from Mr. Russo about General Gotovina's active participation in the Brioni meeting, and how he implemented the plan formed at that meeting by commanding a shelling attack directed at civilian populated areas in the Krajina aimed at driving out the Krajina Serbs. The shelling attack was only the beginning of General Gotovina's participation in the JCE. Following that attack, as his forces entered towns and villages in the Krajina, they participated in a large-scale campaign of looting and burning that forced out many of the Serbs who had not fled the shelling, and prevented the return of those who had. International observers concluded, based on the scale of the destruction and its systematic and prolonged nature, that this campaign was carried out pursuant to orders or silent approval of the Croatian leadership. And with respect to General Gotovina, they were correct. General Gotovina implemented and fostered a climate of impunity and official inaction that encouraged and condoned his subordinates' crimes by deliberately failing to take genuine measures to prevent or stop them. In their brief, the Gotovina Defence claim that the Chamber cannot reach this conclusion because General Gotovina issued orders that, on their face, were aimed at preventing his subordinates burning and looting. Mr. Tieger has already identified the legal errors based on a mischaracterisation of the Blaskic case that ground this claim, and has explained that these orders must be assessed in context and in light of the evidence as a whole. The evidence, as a whole, demonstrates that General Gotovina's orders to prevent looting and burning were aimed at masking his acceptance of those crimes, not at preventing them. And what is that context? Well, as we have explained at paragraph 146 and 147 of our brief, immediately before Operation Storm, General Gotovina's subordinates were looting and burning in Grahovo and Glamoc, even after the Split Military District had ordered them to stop. In this context, the only preventative measure with any substantial likelihood of success would be to identify and punish or at least remove from combat those who were looting or burning. General Gotovina did nothing aimed at achieving either measure. Instead, he ordered all forces involved in Operation Summer to remain in position and await further orders. He issued instructions to promote and reward soldiers and officers, and he order the dissemination of a false report on the use of phosphoric shells to cover up the burning of Grahovo and Glamoc. I refer you to our final brief at paragraphs 149 to 151. Thus, on the eve of Storm, General Gotovina sent this message to his subordinates: I will not punish you for your crimes and I will take steps to cover them up. In this context, he must have expected his subordinates to repeat their looting and burning, regardless of contrary orders. His subordinates had already done that and they had gotten away with it. Yet in the attack orders attachments, he simply repeated the same instruction to prevent looting and burning that had already failed. On top of that, General Gotovina included no measures to monitor the implementation of these instructions. He also took no measures to secure their implementation, except for his order to OG commanders to station MUP and MP in large towns to secure the town and important buildings. As we have pointed out in paragraphs 21 to 23 of our brief, this instruction, which was consistent with the common purpose, had a measure of success, as large towns and important buildings were practically the only structures relatively spared from otherwise total devastation. Apart from this particular measure, it is clear that General Gotovina expected his orders to prevent looting and burning to fail, and when they did, he did not want to know about it or do anything about it. Any uncertainty about that is resolved by his response to the ensuing wave of looting and burning carried out in contravention of those orders. By at least 6 August, General Gotovina's comments at the Knin fortress and the independent evidence of the situation in and around the town at this time show that General Gotovina knew his orders were totally ineffective. Was he generally concerned about stopping these crimes or punishing the perpetrators? At this time, with his subordinate commanders sitting all around him, he would have taken immediate steps to find out why his orders had not been followed. He would have held his subordinate commanders accountable for failing to implement his orders. He would have initiated concrete measures such as detention, disciplinary punishments, arrests, and curfews to bring his subordinates under control and prevent further crimes. And crucially, he would have taken steps to secure the implementation of his orders. General Gotovina did none of those things either on the 6th of August or at any time in the ensuing days and weeks, despite a constant flow of information that his orders continued to be disobeyed on a massive scale. In this context, his repeated incantations over the following days of the same hollow order that had already failed at least twice were not genuine. Barkovic and Theunens both confirmed what any teacher, parent or other authority figure knows and what an experienced commander like General Gotovina certainly knew: Reissuing the same failed order is not an effective measure. A commander who becomes aware his orders are not being implemented must take steps to find out what has gone wrong and secure the implementation of his orders. I refer you to paragraphs 193 to 195 of our brief. I will turn now to a few of the purported preventative measures the Gotovina Defence relies upon in an effort to demonstrate that General Gotovina took genuine steps to prevent or punish crimes. One of these is General Gotovina's 9 August instruction, documented at page 95 of the operational diary, to photograph and video record criminal acts, which can you see on this slide. There are at least three reasons that this order does not reflect a genuine attempt to prevent or punish crimes. First, General Gotovina does not actually instruct anyone to implement this claimed order. And the evidence at paragraph 175 of our brief demonstrates it was not, in fact, implemented. Secondly, General Gotovina's subordinates were already committing their crimes openly. It would have been fanciful to think that photographing soldiers who are already committing crimes in front of their commanders and with their acquiescence would be an effective measure. Third, and most importantly, General Gotovina made this comment at a meeting with his subordinate commanders. Were he genuinely interested in stopping these crimes, he would have ordered those commanders to detain and punish those caught looting and burning, not take photographs of them. In short, this order is a farce. Its only utility is to demonstrate to this Chamber the deliberate nature of General Gotovina's failure to take simple measures to ensure the crime wave was stopped and his subordinates punished. At paragraph 765 of their brief, the Gotovina Defence continues to claim that the demobilisation of criminals was a necessary and reasonable measure of punishment. They assert that the Prosecution has offered no evidence to justify its position that it was not. Well, it is up to the Chamber to determine whether or not demobilisation in the circumstances of this case was a necessary and reasonable measure, and it is proper for the Prosecution to make submissions on this, as we have done at paragraphs 236 to 237 of our brief. The Gotovina Defence also claims that Lausic described demobilisation as the strongest measure in dealing with undisciplined soldiers. That mischaracterises Lausic's evidence. As you can see, at paragraph 210 of Exhibit P2159, Lausic described using the threat of demobilisation as leverage to maintain discipline among reserve units. This does not support the proposition that criminals within the HV could be appropriately punished through their simple demobilisation. At paragraphs 771 to 737, the Gotovina Defence has argued that General Gotovina's purported measures to prevent and punish crime were effective and that General Gotovina believed they were effective by claiming that: "There is no evidence of any HV units engaging in unlawful activity in Croatia after 18 August." The annexes to the Prosecution's final brief demonstrate this is false. Furthermore, as we pointed out at paragraphs 185 to 189 of our brief, this continued criminal activity was repeatedly reported to General Gotovina. The Gotovina Defence also rely on Exhibit D1286, Budimir's 7 September report to the MP administration, which can you see here. In this report, Budimir stated that: "After the initial four to five days," all instances of setting fire to houses were prevented. The Gotovina Defence claims that Budimir would have reported this to General Gotovina, indicating to him that the measures he took as of 18 August were effective. First, as you can see, Budimir only mentions burning and says nothing about looting, contrary to what is stated at paragraph 772 of the Defence brief. But, in any event, Budimir's statement is absurd. It is contradicted by voluminous and readily observable evidence of burning far beyond the initial four to five days, as Budimir and General Gotovina knew full well. For example, as you can see here, on the 18th of August, as recorded in P71, page 116, the military police reported to the Split MD command that "the burning of houses and killing of cattle is being continued." Had Budimir reported to General Gotovina what is stated in Budimir's 7 September report, it should have alarmed General Gotovina that his own MP battalion commander was willing to present such a blatantly false picture of the crime situation. At paragraph 591 of their brief, the Defence sets out a complete list of measures they claim were aimed at preventing and punishing crime in an attempt to undermine the conclusion that General Gotovina contributed to the JCE through his failure to act. I do not have time to address them all today. Suffice it to say that when the evidence underlying these purported measures is contrasted with the evidence demonstrating General Gotovina's broad prevention and punishment powers, and his exercise of those powers in matters unrelated to the indictment, this list merely highlights General Gotovina's failure to take genuine measures aimed at preventing and punishing his subordinates' crimes. The evidence, as a whole, demonstrates that General Gotovina intended the crimes committed through looting and burning and contributed to this aspect of the common purpose through his deliberate, persistent inaction. At the very least, the evidence shows that he was aware that these crimes were foreseeable consequences of the execution of the common purpose, and willingly took the risk they might be committed in its execution. I will move on now to discuss General Gotovina's mens rea for the crime of murder. Although the Prosecution relies principally on the mode of liability of JCE, the Prosecution also relies on several alternative modes of liability. Although the mens rea standards for these modes vary somewhat, all are based on an awareness standard. I refer the Chamber to paragraphs 122 to 129 and 199 to 205 of our brief, which discusses the factors and evidence demonstrating that each of these standards is satisfied. Rather than repeat that summary today, I will address some of the Defence submissions on that evidence and those factors. As a general matter, the Defence have separated out individual pieces of information and put forward arguments aimed at showing that each particular piece of information did not serve to notify General Gotovina that his subordinates were committing murder. This approach is flawed in two respects. First, the Defence applies an actual knowledge standard, a standard which is not necessary to satisfy any of the applicable mens rea standards in this case. Second, this approach improperly addresses the evidence in a piecemeal manner rather than considering the evidence as a whole, and thereby fails to consider the cumulative effect these pieces of information had on General Gotovina's awareness. Bearing in mind this generally erroneous approach, I will address a few of the Defence claims about these individual pieces of information. The first relates to General Gotovina's comments at Brioni about the difficulty of keeping his subordinates on a leash. At paragraph 693 of their brief, the Defence relies on General Gotovina's later use of the term "leash" in a different context to support their assertion that this comment was about troop morale. This doesn't make sense. The Chamber should interpret General Gotovina's remarks in the context in which they were given, and General Gotovina made those remarks in response to Tudjman's comments which included his reminder to "please remember how many Croatian towns and villages have been destroyed, but that is still not the situation in Knin today." Another Defence claim is that General Gotovina's knowledge of the attitude of his subordinates is limited to the 3rd Battalion of the 126th Regiment, because that was the unit he specifically mentioned at Brioni. Well, regardless of how one interprets this particular comment, General Gotovina knew this attitude of revenge was a broader phenomenon. Revenge and hatred were the justifications he gave to internationals when they confronted him with crimes. Furthermore, it was common knowledge that the Home Guard units were made up of soldiers who had been expelled from the Krajina and had otherwise suffered at the hands of the Krajina Serb regime. It is a simple matter of common sense to connect that fact to the propensity for revenge and the corresponding need for extra measures of monitoring and control in the context of Operation Storm. Mladen Barkovic was more or less stating the obvious when he drew those connections, at page 20175 of the transcript, which can you see here. He testified that because Home Guard unit members had had their properties in the Krajina destroyed, the situation required "a high degree of strict control to make sure that such individuals did not engage in misdeeds." And the same logical connection between Home Guards, revenge and crime was made by General Gotovina only assistant commander for political affairs in his 13 August report, D810, which you can see here. Noting that arson was most often carried out by Home Guards, he stated: "It should be assumed that their motive is revenge." This evidence contradicts the Defence claim in paragraph 695 that there is no evidence that Home Guard units harboured particular animosity towards the civilian population beyond what could reasonably be expected in wartime circumstances. At paragraph 693 of their brief, the Defence makes another false claim that the 3rd Battalion of the 126th Regiment did not even participate in the Grahovo operation. The entries at pages 2, 18, 29, 39, 51, and 63 of P71 make clear that the 126th Regiment, and, in particular, its 3rd Battalion, did participate in this operation. Furthermore, as you can see from this 13 August MP report, Exhibit P2665, this unit also participated in burning the houses in Grahovo in an organised fashion. And this latter exhibit also demonstrates that the Defence claim at paragraph 695 of their brief that there is no evidence in the record of any Home Guard unit of the Split MD committing any crime against Serbs or Serb property at any time prior to Storm is also false. At paragraph 708 of their brief, the Defence claim that General Gotovina's knowledge of his subordinates' property destruction and looting cannot constitute inquiry notice of murder and mistreatment based on a claimed fundamental principle that knowledge must relate to specific crimes. This claim is not substantiated by the jurisprudence the Gotovina Defence relies upon. Although the Krnojelac Appeals Judgement held, at paragraph 155, that a commander must be in possession of sufficiently alarming information to put him on notice of the particular offence with which he is charged. There is no rule that the sufficiently alarming information standard is only met where the commander has actual knowledge of his subordinates committing past acts of that particular offence." The jurisprudence is clear that whether an accused had sufficiently alarming information to constitute inquiry notice must be assessed in the particular circumstances of the case and that relevant factors are not limited to knowledge of past crimes. For example, at paragraph 238 of the Celebici appeals judgement, the Chamber held that: "A military commander who has received information that some of the soldiers under his command have a violent or unstable character or have been drinking prior to being sent on mission may be considered as having the required knowledge." In this case, a number of factors, including but not limited to General Gotovina's knowledge of his subordinates burning and looting are relevant to assessing his awareness of the substantial likelihood or at least the risk of murder once Operation Storm began. Furthermore, in the circumstances of this case, the line between crimes against Serb property and crimes against Serbs themselves is a thin one. The evidence shows soldiers torching homes on a massive scale, frequently using fuel or other means to accelerate the burning, sometimes burning down entire villages at a time. Burning of this nature is an act of violence directed not just at the homes and villages themselves but at anyone unlucky enough to be in or around them. So, for example, when it was reported to the Split MD command on 29 July that all units in the area save two were burning houses in Grahovo, and that "the entire Grahovo was on fire," and that's P71, pages 49 to 50, this was a clear signal of the disregard those units, which included General Gotovina's so-called professional units, had for the lives and safety of Serb civilians. In short, Your Honours, the prospects for the Krajina Serbs who did not flee the shelling were grim. Gotovina's forces had shelled their homes and villages for two days. Heading toward them were thousands of armed soldiers, many of whom were clearly willing to commit crimes that they did not expect to be punished for and willing to risk the lives of Serbs who happened to be in their path of destruction. Many were also fueled by revenge, aimed at those they perceived responsible for expelling them from the Krajina. General Gotovina knew all this when he ordered those soldiers to attack towns and villages in the Krajina, and consequently, he must have been aware of the substantial likelihood or at least the risk of some of his subordinates murdering and mistreating Serbs in those towns and villages. And the evidence shows that is exactly what happened. Your Honours, I've reached a point in my presentation where it would be convenient to take a break if that suits the Chamber.

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Before the break I had summarised the dangers that General Gotovina's subordinates posed to the Krajina Serbs who did not flee the shelling and Gotovina's awareness of those dangers. And as the evidence --
