utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. Thank you. And as the evidence described in the Prosecution's brief demonstrates, General Gotovina's forces, indeed, murdered dozens of Serbs in the initial days of the ground attack. And evidence of those murders was visible to Murray Dawes and Andries Dreyer who managed to leave the UN compound and move around Knin during those first few days of Storm, before this evidence was cleared away by sanitation efforts. They observed dozens of dead bodies in the streets around Knin, many of whom were civilians showing signs of murder. And I refer you to paragraph 202 of our brief. In addition to describing the dead bodies he saw, at P980, page 9, Dawes added that: "All over the town there was rotten smell which I'll never forget." General Gotovina's exchange with an unknown interlocutor on the 6th of August meeting in Knin, which can you see on this slide, from D792, indicates that he, too, must have seen such dead bodies in and around Knin on the 6th of August. He asks: "Did you restore the town?" The answer: "I did." And he says: "And those dogs, those cats in the street, which are in the middle of the street." And the response: "First we had to collect ..." And there's a further exchange, and the unknown person says: "Well, there was some 150 so far. And General Gotovina says: "I don't care how many there were. I didn't ask you for a figure." Now, regardless of how one interprets General Gotovina's references at this video-recorded meeting to dogs and cats in the middle of the street, it is clear from this exchange that General Gotovina had closely observed the streets around Knin, which were then littered with human remains, and he urgently want those streets cleaned up. And he could not have avoided the stench of death permeating the town at this time or the sound of small arms fire emanating from down-town Knin. And I refer you again to paragraph 202 of our brief. On top of signs pointing specifically to murder, the overall situation in and around Knin on 6 August was one of open and widespread criminality. General Gotovina himself referred to his subordinates as barbarians and vandals. Hill's description of Knin on 6 August, at page 22 of P292, which can you see here, illustrates the nature of the crime spree that General Gotovina observed. "Soldiers were looting everywhere, absolutely everywhere. They were drinking, they were firing. Places were on fire ... everywhere you go, there's soldiers stealing cars. And [sic] any car that wasn't destroyed or run over by a tank, or whatever, they were stealing." Even if he didn't actually see any of his subordinates kill or mistreat Serbs in Knin, the total criminality among his subordinates that General Gotovina witnessed on 6 August heightened his awareness of the dangers his subordinates posed to the Krajina Serbs in the area. At paragraph 745 of their brief, the Gotovina Defence claims that: "Both political affairs and SIS reported to Gotovina that civilians had been property treated by HV forces." They rely on two reports. One of those is P1134, and you can see the relevant extract on this slide. The report does state that: "The civilians found in the town were treated properly and professionally by the army." However, the report also states that HV members demolished shops, ran tanks over cars, and drove around Knin in seized cars, drunkenly shooting and threatening people's lives. The contradictory statements in this report would have signalled to General Gotovina not only that his subordinates were drunkenly shooting their weapons and threatening lives, but also that HV officials did not consider this behaviour to constitute improper treatment of civilians. Were General Gotovina genuinely concerned about the safety of Serbs in the area, this report would not have reassured him. To the contrary, this report is a classic example of the alarming information that should have triggered General Gotovina to make further inquiries, inquiries that he chose not to make. In paragraph 703, the Defence claims the Chamber should not consider media reports of murder and mistreatment as notice evidence. They claim, as can you see here, that the Prosecution has failed to provide a single piece of evidence that General Gotovina read contemporaneous media reports of crimes. The evidence of General Gotovina reading media reports is clear, as can you see from this extract of P407. On 13 September, General Gotovina wrote to Cervenko, stating: "I would like to take this opportunity to cite a statement made to journalists by Mr. Roberts which reads, 'The Croatian Army is burning, looting and violating human rights.'" General Gotovina does not use the word "murder" here, but this was yet another piece of information adding to his awareness relating to murder and mistreatment among his subordinates. And, indeed, Mr. Roberts had referred specifically to murder in his media statement a few days before this, as this 1st of September UN radio report, P712, makes clear. It quotes Alun Roberts stating that killing, looting and burning of houses are continuing, often by members of the Croatian Army. At paragraph 710 of their brief, the Defence addresses General Lausic's 16 September report, D567, copied to General Gotovina which, as can you see here, reported the occurrence of HV murders in the liberated area. I apologise for the typo on this slide. It results from a typo in the English translation of this document. The Defence claims that this report: "Reassured every MD commander that the MPs were taking all appropriate measures to prevent and punish crime by HV wrongdoers." Now whether or not the measures described in D567 were appropriate, this report is direct notice to General Gotovina of HV murders in the Krajina after Storm. Furthermore, this report could not possibly have reassured General Gotovina that MPs were effectively preventing murders or other HV crimes. After stating that the MP was unable to completely prevent crimes, Lausic stated in this report that commanders of HV units could make a "great contribution" to improving security situations in the liberated areas, and he proposed that measures be taken to assure the line of command within HV units. And that's at page 10, D567. In sum, General Gotovina received persistent and escalating signs of murder and mistreatment by his subordinates. If his actual knowledge of such crimes was delayed, this was as a result of his choice not to take simple and obvious steps to follow up on these signs. I'll now address General Gotovina's superior responsibility, starting with his effective control. I'll first address the Chamber's request, under point 4 of its e-mail to the parties, to respond to Defence arguments that General Gotovina did not have effective control based on claims about layers of commands, and the nature of Home Guard conscripts, recently mobilised soldiers, and the NCO corps. First, the mere fact of intervening of layers of command is irrelevant to the question of effective control. As the Oric Appeals Chamber made clear at paragraph 20 of its judgement, the existence of intermediary subordinates is immaterial as a matter of law. What matters is whether a superior had the material ability to prevent or punish his criminally responsible subordinate, and that is a matter of evidence. At paragraph 626, the Defence claim the Prosecution must establish that each commander in the chain of command possessed effective control over his subordinate commanders. The Oric Appeals Judgement makes clear that this is false. What the Prosecution must establish is that General Gotovina had the material power to prevent or punish his criminally responsible subordinates. The Defence also claims, at paragraph 621, that it was the primary job of commanders at the scene to prevent or punish soldiers. Apart from the fact that this is not supported by the legal authorities or evidence they cite, it does not address the question of General Gotovina's effective control, which is simply whether he had the material ability to prevent or punish his subordinates. And for the same reasons, the Defence claims about inexperienced NCOs or the breakdown of authority in a particular unit do not demonstrate that General Gotovina lacked the material ability to prevent or punish those soldiers. It is useful to look at an example here, and the Gotovina Defence provides one at paragraphs 641 to 643 of their brief. Here, the Defence points to this extract from Exhibit D984, a report from the OG West assistant commander for SIS, stating that the commander of 134th lacked the necessary authority to implement orders and that the members of the unit were continuously destroying property. The Defence relies on this evidence to claim that this unit was "not under effective control." But this assertion confuses the fact that a unit is out of control with a lack of effective control, but these are two completely different questions. The only relevant question is whether General Gotovina had the material power to prevent the property destruction committed by the 134th members or punish them for these crimes. As a Colonel General and commander of the military district, General Gotovina had enormous and varied powers to prevent and punish these crimes, including measures which did not depend upon the ability of the 134th commander to implement orders. Orders General Gotovina actually issued concerning matters unrelated to the charged crimes illustrate the measures available to him to prevent and punish these crimes, crimes, which, in this case were reported to him. For example, he could have ordered the 134th commander, the OG West commander or any other officer under his command to establish a system of monitoring, identifying and punishing perpetrators, as he did in Exhibit D655. He could have suspended and punished any of his subordinate commanders for failing to follow his orders, as he did in P1033. He could have ordered a military police unit to the area to monitor and police the regiment, as he did in Exhibit P1142. He could have ordered the military police to arrest the perpetrators and initiate criminal proceedings, as he did at page 7 of P1013, and page 3 of P1126. He could have set up a commission to investigate the 134th Regiment and initiate disciplinary, criminal and preventative measures, as he did in P1013 and P1019. He could have established a security force to secure the towns and villages in the 134th Regiment's AOR, as he did in Exhibit D773. Or he could formed an intervention unit to restrict and control the movement of the 134th Regiment members, as he did in P1142. With respect to all the above orders, General Gotovina could have taken measures to monitor and ensure their implementation, as he did in many of the examples I just cited. General Gotovina took no such measures, either with respect to the crimes of the 134th Regiment, or any other charged crimes. Although we are focussed here on effective control, while we're on this example of the 134th Home Guards, I would like to digress for a moment to look at the Defence claim that General Gotovina took the necessary and reasonable measures in this instance. Those measures are identified at paragraphs 761 to 762 of their brief, and they are: 1, demobilising members of the units; 2, Colonel Fuzul's 19 August order, Exhibit D650, to take measures to restore discipline; and 3, General Gotovina's order, Exhibit D985, forming a commission to "check and list the war booty of the 134th Home Guard Regiment" and report back to him. I have addressed that demobilisation was not a necessary or reasonable punishment measure. Colonel Fuzul's order essentially repeats numerous prior failed orders, without any measures to monitor or secure its implementation and, therefore, was neither necessary nor reasonable in the circumstances. With respect to General Gotovina's war booty order, the Prosecution has explained, at paragraphs 169 to 173 of its brief, how these orders were not even aimed at preventing or punishing crimes, let alone necessary or reasonable measures. In any event, the report to the Split MD was of property destruction. So a commission to list war booty could not even arguably be responsive to that report. Turning back to the issue of effective control, the evidence shows that General Gotovina's war booty order was effective, as this extract from page 19 of D987, a 30 October 1995 Main Staff report to the -- indicates. The report states that the war booty of the 134th Regiment was duly and completely registered and, in accordance with the Split MD command, part of it was handed over to other units. The Defence claim at paragraph 640 that large numbers of mobilised soldiers made it "exceeding difficult" for General Gotovina to exercise effective control. First, this is an theoretical proposition, since General Gotovina never tried to exercise the measures available to him. Second, all the measures I listed above applied equally to reserves and recently mobilised soldiers. Third, at the time of Operation Storm, General Gotovina never reported to his superiors that mobilisation or the level of experience of his NCO corps caused problems with effective control or command and control, more generally. To the contrary, as Exhibit P1132, General Gotovina's 15 August assessment, makes clear, General Gotovina noted the successful completion of tasks by his units. He stated that military discipline and combat morale was exceptionally high, and declared that command and control was uninterrupted and at the required level. The only mention he made of NCOs in this assessment was his remark that proposals for NCO commendations would be submitted later. And the only problems he identified in this report related to communications equipment. In a similar analysis he produced a month later, Exhibit P2585, General Gotovina again stated that command and control functioned relatively well, and again, he made no mention of any problems with NCOs, mobilisation or ill-discipline. The discrepancy between General Gotovina's satisfaction with command and control and military discipline within his units and these same units' obvious lack of discipline relating to crimes against Serbs and their property is yet another illustration of General Gotovina's lack of concern about these crimes. Exhibit D987, which contains a 25 October report of a political affairs inspection of the Split MD, more explicitly reveals the lack of concern over military discipline relating to crimes versus that relating to combat tasks. That report states that there is a difference in the level of discipline for the execution of tasks versus the treatment of property. It states that property crimes still persist due to undisciplined contact and a lack of sanctions, and it observes that there is no systematic monitoring, analysing or proposing measures to prevent such incidents. In this case, there are three primary factors demonstrating General Gotovina's effective control over all his subordinates, including reserves, Home Guards and recently mobilised units. First, and most importantly, General Gotovina had significant material powers of prevention and punishment available but did not use them to address his subordinates' crimes. Two, his subordinates generally followed his orders and General Gotovina had the ability to ensure compliance with them. And I refer you to paragraph 206 of our final brief. And, three, General Gotovina expressed his satisfaction with his command and control over his subordinates and their level of military discipline. The Defence claim, in paragraph 637, that General Gotovina's issuance of failed orders to prevent crimes - orders which he failed to monitor or enforce - evidences a lack of effective control is circular and it is flawed. Because General Gotovina chose not to act to enforce these orders, non-compliance with those same orders does not show a lack of effective control. And I refer the Chamber to the Strugar Appeals Judgement at paragraphs 257 to 258, where they address a similar issue. Contrary to the Defence claims in paragraphs 624 and 774 of their brief, whether or not General Gotovina's "normal duties included monitoring specific disciplinary sanctions imposed by lower-level commanders" is irrelevant, as it does not address the question of reasonably available measures. To the extent his material ability to monitor such disciplinary measures is relevant, General Gotovina did monitor such disciplinary measures when he wanted to be informed about them, as illustrated by P1013 and P1034. The claim in paragraph 624 that Barkovic "testified that a commander is expected to monitor his own level of command and two levels below him," again, does not address reasonably available measures and it mischaracterises Barkovic's evidence. This slide shows that evidence. Barkovic's answer, at page 20186, when he was asked to confirm that a commander should not simply reissue an earlier failed order, Barkovic was not saying here that General Gotovina need only ensure that commanders two levels down from him were not committing crimes, but, rather, that he was required to take measures at least through those two levels to get to the bottom of the problem and ensure that appropriate conduct was achieved. As a general matter, the Defence submissions on effective control are replete with claims that General Gotovina's position and function minimised or absolved his responsibility for his subordinates' crimes. For example, they argue that General Gotovina was "not burdened with security obligations" because he was conducting military operations in Bosnia. That's at paragraph 652. Similar claims can be found at paragraphs 660 to 662. Apart from the fact that these claims are largely not supported by the evidence or the legal authorities cited in support, they confuse arguments about the reasonableness of the measures General Gotovina took with the question of effective control, which is simply whether or not General Gotovina had the material ability to prevent and punish his subordinates. The evidence cited in support of these Defence arguments does not support the proposition that those prevention or punishment powers were somehow diminished or abrogated in the circumstances. That concludes my submissions on effective control. As I have already discussed General Gotovina's actual and inquiry notice, I will move on to discuss his failure to take necessary and reasonable measures. Earlier in my submissions I discussed how General Gotovina's purported orders to prevent crimes were not necessary and reasonable in the circumstances. So I will now address some of the specific arguments raised in the Defence brief. The Oric Appeals Chamber stated clearly at paragraph 177 of its judgement: "... that 'necessary' measures are the measures appropriate for the superior to discharge his obligation (showing that he genuinely tried to prevent or punish) and 'reasonable' measures are those reasonably following within the material powers of the superior ..." And the Chamber emphasised that this is the only relevant legal standard. The Defence has incorrectly attempted to apply a different standard at paragraph 711 of its brief. Also incorrect is the claim at paragraph 715 that a different legal standard applies to operational commanders. At paragraph 746 to 748, the Defence makes the unfounded claim that General Gotovina had no duty to punish crimes that the military police were aware of. This argument is based on General Gotovina's alleged duty within the "Croatian system" which is irrelevant to his duties under international law. In any event, it ignores his duties, even under the Croatian system, to ensure discipline among his subordinates. I refer to you paragraph 211 of our brief. The further claim that this proposition is supported by the Hadzihasanovic Trial Judgement improperly attempts to turn a specific factual finding in that case into a general legal proposition. In the same vein, at paragraphs 774 through 783, the Defence claim that General Gotovina "discharged his disciplinary duties by ensuring that there is a system established to address discipline concerns and that the system functions." This does not address the question as to whether or not he took measures reasonably within his material powers, demonstrating that he genuinely tried to prevent or punish crimes in the circumstances. In any event, this claim is based on a mischaracterisation of both Deverell's evidence and the Boskoski Appeals Judgement. It also does not account for General Gotovina's focussed interventions in that disciplinary system to address matters other than the crimes with which he is charged, as illustrated by P1019, P1013, and P1034. And I note in passing that with respect to P1013, he issued the orders in that document in late August and early September, a time when the Defence claim he was too focussed on the ongoing battle in Bosnia to be expected to bother himself with disciplinary matters. At paragraph 660 to 662, the Defence claims that General Gotovina justifiably relied on others, particularly the MP, SIS and PD, to discharge his obligation to prevent and punish. And, at paragraph 749, they claim that through his remarks at the 6 August meeting in Knin, General Gotovina satisfied his duty to punish crimes, at least in part, by "alerting" these organs about crime and reminding them that it was "their duty to enforce the rules of armed forces." I have already addressed what one would have expected General Gotovina to do and say at this meeting were he genuinely interested in preventing and punishing crimes. In any event, these claims again are largely based on General Gotovina's alleged duties within the Croatian system. Furthermore, these claims are based on General Gotovina's own personal interpretation of his duties versus the duties of the MP, SIS and PD that he expressed on videotape after witnessing the disastrous behaviour of his subordinates. His interpretation is wrong. First, it is contradicted by the evidence showing that it was General Gotovina's duty, even under the Croatian system, to command and control and ensure discipline among his subordinates. I refer you to P1187, Article 5; P1116, Article 49; and references at footnote 651 of our brief. Secondly, his interpretation ignores General Gotovina's power and authority over these very organs to assist him in fulfilling his duties. The Defence claims at paragraph 607(G) that SIS, PD, and MP were not under General Gotovina's command. And at paragraph 750, they claim that all he could do was implore them to act. The Prosecution has addressed the evidence that shows conclusively that General Gotovina had command authority over the MP and the ability to order them to take crime prevention and punishment measures at paragraphs 239 to 269 of its brief, and I will not address that topic today. I will address the novel claim that General Gotovina was not in command of the SIS or PD. General Gotovina's own staff included assistant commanders for both services. There is no merit to the claim that General Gotovina did not command these members of his own staff, and the evidence is clear that he did. I refer you to general evidence at P1187, Article 5; P1113, pages 89 to 102; and specific examples at D792, pages 3 to 4; P1126; D201; P982, page 1; D985; and P2349, page 3. In any event, the role of SIS and PD was limited to tasks such as monitoring, collecting information, and providing advice. It was for this reason that Theunens found it "unusual that General Gotovina casted blame on these services." As you can see from this slide, at page 12771, Theunens explained that these services do not have command authority over the perpetrators and that it was up to the operational commander to use the advice he receives from the PD and SIS to issue orders and verify their implementation. The OG North assistant PD commander made a similar observation in his 10 August report, D982. He noted that commanders were not taking appropriate measures to prevent arson and destruction in large towns and settlements, and then were elegantly shifting the blame to the PD, SIS and MP "who do not have the authority to give orders." As my final point on this issue, Your Honours, although the determination of necessary and reasonable measures is a matter of evidence, I refer the Chamber to a useful list of relevant factors, at paragraph 378 of the Strugar Trial Judgement. I would like to conclude by addressing a common them that runs throughout the General Gotovina Defence brief. This is the claim that General Gotovina was somehow too senior in the military hierarchy for him to bear responsibility for the crimes of his subordinates. This theme arises in the JCE context at paragraphs 600 to 601, and arises repeatedly in the discussion of superior responsibility. I have already addressed General Gotovina's tremendous prevention and punishment powers, arising from his senior position, that show his effective control over perpetrators regardless of their level in the hierarchy. I have also discussed how he failed to exercise those powers, and how his position at the top of the command chain did not mean that he satisfied his duty to prevent or punish by simply double-checking that there was a functioning system of military discipline and then expecting others to deal with his subordinates' crime wave. In relation to JCE, contrary to the suggestion at paragraph 601 of the Defence brief, the Brdjanin Appeals Judgement does not support the proposition that the mere existence of intervening layers of command between an accused and the physical perpetrators within a hierarchical structure such as the HV precludes a finding of JCE liability. To the contrary, although the sufficiency of the link is a factual matter that must be determined in the circumstances of the case, the Appeals Chamber has found relationships of command and control sufficient to establish such a link in the case of senior leaders. And I refer you to paragraphs 187 and 210 of the Martic Appeals Judgement. On the facts of this case, at paragraph 600, the Defence claims that because General Gotovina was the highest ranking commander in the Split MD, JCE liability is precluded, due to an alleged remoteness between his failure to act and the commission of crimes. That argument turns the reality of this case on its head. Colonel General Gotovina was a respected and highly effective military commander. The evidence show that he demanded and ensured compliance with his orders when he was interested in enforcing them. He commanded 30.000 troops in the largest military operation in Croatia's history, and from a purely combat-related perspective, executed that operation skillfully and successfully. Through his leadership and command, General Gotovina set the command climate for the entire Military District. He insisted on military discipline in combat-related matters all the way down to the lowest level soldier, while ignoring the rampant criminality among those soldiers directed at Serbs and their property. General Gotovina permitted this climate of impunity to flow down his chain of command and permeate the entire Military District. His persistent failure to take measures genuinely aimed at preventing or stopping his subordinates' crimes was not remote from those crimes. To the contrary, it was a crucial contributing factor to the breakdown in discipline that allowed those crimes to be committed as a matter of course and become the rule rather than the exception to the rule within his Military District. That concludes my submissions, Your Honour. I would like to thank the Court and pass the floor to Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be dealing with the Cermak part of the Prosecution's submissions. Just as a preliminary matter before I start to answer questions number 1 and questions number 8 that were received from the Chamber last week, just to provide the following answers. Question number 1, regarding footnote 859, we confirm that the Chamber correctly understood the acts underlying the crime of persecution that are relied upon by the Prosecution in respect of General Cermak. And for question number 8, which is the sentence contained in paragraph 361 of the Prosecution's brief, and associated footnote 1263, the text of that sentence, the word "and" located between the words "investigate" and "crimes" should be replaced with the word "the." And turning to the presentation, I will provide an overview of the three fundamental parts of the Prosecution case against General Cermak. Namely, General Cermak's presidential appointment to the JCE and his related enhanced authority; 2, General Cermak's intentional disregard for his duty as Knin garrison commander to establish order and maintain discipline within his area of responsibility, and this failure was in stark contrast to General Cermak's successful mobilisation and command of the resources that he used to immediately repopulate the liberated areas with ethnic Croat civilians in order to permanently displace the Krajina Serbs; and, 3, General Cermak's intentional obstruction of the international community in order to cover up the crimes being committed against Serbs and to allow these crimes to continue. Obviously, Your Honours, I will not attempt to recite in detail the evidence contained in the Prosecution brief. However, I will highlight certain issues and address particular issues raised in the Cermak Defence brief such as General Cermak being a mere conduit and the impact of his admissions that certain crimes were committed. I'll turn to his appointment. President Tudjman personally recruited General Cermak into the JCE and appointed him Knin garrison commander on 5 August 1995. General Cermak was a trusted political insider and he operated under the auspices and direction of President Tudjman from Knin. These are contained in the -- the Prosecution's brief at paragraphs 289 to 298. General Cermak's appointment cannot be understood as anything other than extraordinary given the circumstances under which it occurred. President Tudjman was the commander of the Croatian forces engaged in Operation Storm and would have quickly learned that, as planned, Serbs had start to the flee in response to the illegal shelling campaign. On 4 August, after receiving a progress report on Storm from Minister Susak, but before the HV had liberated Knin and before any assessment of any damage to infrastructure or public works, President Tudjman had decided to personally seek out Mr. Cermak and only Mr. Cermak. See, for instance, D1678 at paragraphs 8 to 9, and Prosecution brief at paragraph 295. In a telephone conversation with Mr. Cermak, President Tudjman reveals his secret location and requested a face-to-face meeting. See, for instance, P2525, page 9 and page 65. During their private meeting on 5 August, President Tudjman issued an oral order reactivating Colonel General Cermak and sent him to Knin as garrison commander but with the additional authority to execute his presidential assignment. The Defence assert that General Cermak had become somewhat of a political outsider after leaving public office in 1993. And in their brief they assert that he was someone who had little contact with President Tudjman from Knin; had returned to public service in August 1995 with limited powers as a garrison commander; and that he had focussed his attention on reconnecting the water, telephones, electricity, and passing on messages from the international community. This is contained in the Defence brief in part 3, in paragraphs 77, 78, 116, 136, and on. Such assertions are inconsistent with the weight of the evidence, particularly considering the following facts. First, only a trusted insider would have been summoned for a private audience with the Supreme Commander of Croatian forces in the midst of what was deemed Croatia's most important military offensive. The need for a private face-to-face meeting between these long time political allies the day after they had been able to communicate by telephone, and in light of the fact that they were able to meet publicly the day after this private meeting, suggests that their brief meeting in Zagreb was necessary in order to conduct private matters that were to remain outside of the public eye. Second, General Cermak continued to communicate with the president and the office of the president while he was in Knin, even travelling back to Zagreb to meet with the president on occasion. For instance, D618 at page 1. General Cermak was also in regular communication with other JCE members during this period, including Minister Jarnjak and Generals Gotovina and Markac. And I refer you to the Prosecution's brief at paragraphs 291, 347, 367, 370. The slide on the screen is in reference to Exhibit P2525, page 23, and page -- and Exhibit P2532, page 42. When asked if he could communicate with President Tudjman after his appointment, General Cermak responded: "Of course, I could talk to the president." He also said: "I was more connected to the office of the president. Because I went down there with special tasks from him." The next slide is in reference to Exhibit P2527, page 2. General Cermak's enhanced military status was also reflected in his meeting with General Cervenko on 5 August, and the fact that the Chief of the Main Staff also took the time in the midst of Operation Storm to meet permanently with the man he described as "the president's personal man of confidence." Third, the low-ranking post of garrison commander was at odds with Mr. Cermak's status as a former assistant minister of defence, the former minister of economy, a presidential advisor, a very senior HDZ member, as well as with his newly reactivated rank of Colonel General in the Croatian Army. Fourth, General Cermak's position of authority, trust, and insider status was displayed during his introduction and praise of President Tudjman on 26 August in Knin, where he stood shoulder to shoulder with Tudjman on stage and he declared an end to Croatia's historical burden. In that same exhibit, P473, on page 2 and through to 5, President Tudjman then delivered the Freedom Train speech in which he rejected any notion that Serbs would ever again dominate that region, openly compared Serbs to a cancer in Croatia, and encouraged ethnic Croats to colonise liberated areas. In order to permanently end this historical burden, President Tudjman had granted General Cermak authority and responsibilities that extended well beyond those normally associated with the formal military powers of a garrison commander. General Cermak's enhanced authority emanated from President Tudjman's appointment, and also corresponded precisely with the president's authority over the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Interior, and diplomatic activities. For instance, Witness Granic at transcript page 24647. The combination of authorities granted to General Cermak allowed him to exercise enhanced authority over military and civilian structures on the ground in the aftermath of Storm, which, in turn, allowed General Cermak to use his position as the primary point of contact for Croatian authorities in order to solicit and neutralise the protests and efforts of the international community aimed at protecting Serbs in the Krajina, and also by ensuring that the common criminal purpose would be carried out with minimal international intervention and observation by imposing restrictions on their movements to obstruct international observers. I refer the Chamber to Prosecution's brief at 333 through to 337, and 347 through to 370. General Cermak's appointment to his post of Knin garrison commander also served to ensure that the common criminal purpose to permanently remove the Serbs from the Krajina would be significantly advanced on two specific fronts. First, because he allowed the intended crimes to be committed with impunity within the territory that he controlled; and, second, through his efforts to colonise that area with ethnic Croats. This slide references Exhibit P2715. As garrison commander, General Cermak was responsible for order and discipline of all HV personnel within the territorial boundaries of the garrison, which is shown in green on this map, which I'll put back up on the screen. General Cermak's formal authority as garrison commander is set out in the Prosecution brief at paragraphs 299 through to 314, and paragraphs 319 to 323. During General Cermak's suspect interview, he admitted that a garrison commander was obligated to maintain order and discipline. This slide is in reference to Exhibits P2532, pages 58 to 59; and P2525, at page 57. In the words of General Cermak: "When you have the military accommodated in a place ... and if there is any disorder that happens, that happens, then he," referring to the garrison commander, "can use the military police to discipline them." General Cermak also acknowledged his personal responsibility to prevent and punish crimes committed by soldiers, saying: "In Knin itself, I didn't see destruction and looting. Had I seen anything like that, I would have prevented them. I would have arrested people." Obviously, General Cermak saw the crimes that were being committed by Croatian forces in the aftermath of Storm. In fact, he acknowledged that the situation on the ground was chaotic and urgent. This is in Prosecution's brief at paragraphs 320 and 358. Your Honour, I note the time, if this is a convenient point for a break ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is a convenient time, but give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break now. We resume at 20 minutes past 4.00. And during the break, I'll try to get more detailed information about the time used by the Prosecution until now. Mr. Misetic -- oh, no, you just -- We resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honour, the JCE members intended the crimes to be committed against Serbs in order to drive them out of Knin and the Krajina. As a result of this intention, the Knin garrison commander is going to be placed under pressure from the internationals that were stationed there. He is going to be asked to address the crimes that were going to be committed throughout the area by Croatian forces. It was therefore necessary to recruit a trusted insider to be appointed to this position, and General Cermak immediately supplanted the originally named commander of the garrison, Major Gojevic. That's Prosecution's brief at paragraph 300. As planned, General Cermak took no direct disciplinary action against anyone during his tenure as garrison commander, and he made no meaningful attempt to discharge his duty to control the crimes of burning and looting committed throughout his area of responsibility. This inaction contributed to creating a climate of impunity among Croatian forces which assisted in driving out the remaining Serbs from the Krajina. Prosecution's brief at paragraphs 356 to 362. General Cermak had the material ability to control the military personnel within his area of responsibility, and he could have used the military police and the civilian police that he controlled in Knin to prevent and punish the crimes, as set out in the Prosecution brief at paragraphs 315 to 319, 324 through to 332, 338 to paragraph 345, 360, 364 through to 376. Instead of using these police forces, General Cermak used these police resources at his disposal to advance the JCE. For instance, he used them to guard factories and infrastructure, to look for UN vehicles, and to control the movement of the internationals. General Cermak diverted an inordinate amount of military police and civilian police resources to accomplish these objectives, which in the assessment of General Cermak's own expert, Mr. Albiston, would have had the inevitable effect of reducing police resources for more pressing tasks. See D1776 at paragraph 3.74. During his suspect interview, General Cermak revealed that he intentionally ignored discharging certain duties that were formally attached to his military post and he did this on the instruction of President Tudjman. In this slide, reference is made to Exhibit P2525, page 6 and page 13. In General Cermak's own words: "I never did anything that other commanders of garrisons were doing ... because I was a person of trust for President Tudjman. He knew I would do my job helping normalising." And: "In the garrison, I only did the jobs that I was given by the president." In effect, this meant General Cermak focused his authority and resources on colonising the liberated areas with ethnic Croats, as well as taking steps to obstruct the internationals, rather than to fulfil his promise to the internationals, to discharge his duty to control military personnel committing crimes within his area of responsibility. General Cermak listed return, i.e., Povratak, as one of the tasks that was assigned to him by President Tudjman, although he preferred the euphemism "normalisation" for his involvement in the process of rapid repopulation of the area with ethnic Croats. This is found at P114, page 4. General Cermak was instrumental in accomplishing the process of normalisation which not only served to physically displace the Serbs that had fled, but it also created an inhospitable environment for Serbs generally, thereby continuing the forced exodus and cementing their removal from the Krajina. The Prosecution has set out General Cermak's role in normalisation in paragraphs 289, 333 through to 337, paragraph 346, and paragraphs 371 through to 328 in the Prosecution brief. General Cermak began mobilising resource for normalisation before he even left Zagreb. For instance, on 5 August, General Cermak requested his associates, Major Jonjic, Brigadier Brkic and Brigadier Teskeredzic, to mobilise logistics, sanitation and de-mining teams for use in Knin. In fact, both Jonjic and Brkic's activity reports cover periods beginning from August 5th. General Cermak's immediate action was related to his responsibility for overseeing the sanitation operation, an operation that was aimed at obscuring evidence of murders and clearing a sanitised path for ethnic Croat repopulation. The slide that should be coming up on the screen now is from Exhibit P2525, pages 73 and page 10. In General Cermak' own words: "This," referring to sanitation, "one of my first jobs that I started dealing with." And: "We immediately started with hygiene and sanitation." Although General Cermak confirmed that both civil protection and the HV were involved in sanitation, he maintained that he was tasked with coordinating the process and ensuring that it was carried out. This next slide references Exhibit P2525, page 74. In General Cermak's own words: "The Civilian Defence was there ... we were all there to help each other ... we had to carry out hygiene and sanitation." And there's a question to General Cermak: "But, of course, you were sent by the president as the senior person to coordinate and to ensure that this was done; is that right?" General Cermak answered: "That's right." Your Honours, I will now turn to General Cermak's role in respect of the internationals. The JCE members understood that they risked international condemnation in pursuit of their goal to drive the Serbs out of the Krajina. President Tudjman recognised the need to immediately isolate the international community but without alienating them. This was required in order to prevent and manage, to whatever extent possible under the circumstances, unwanted international intervention or condemnation that might result from the intentional expulsion of ethnic Serbs and the intended and inevitable crimes that would take place. Dealing with the internationals would be a delicate task that would require diplomacy. It required someone senior enough to command the attention and respect of the internationals on the ground, and someone that would be able to pacify the internationals with believable false promises of official action, in order to obscure the true intention behind the crimes and to allow the crimes to continue unabated. In Brioni, Minister of Defence Susak told President Tudjman that it was important to have one person who was in contact with them to be a permanent liaison with the internationals in order to resolve their concerns and to prevent unwanted interventions. This next slide references Exhibit P461 at page 27. Minister Susak said: "Another staff would be for relations with UNCRO, someone who would be a permanent liaison, someone who would be in touch with us and resolve things with them, for us to get instructions, because matters will evolve too rapidly for us to start looking around for them and calling them." President Tudjman ultimately chose General Cermak to fill the role that was discussed during the Brioni meeting and sent him to Knin to become the central Croatian official attached to his office who would be responsible for dealing with the internationals on the grounds. The international community was largely based in Knin, and it became the obvious centre of attention for the mass media and the international organisations on the ground. These internationals were explicitly told that they were to deal directly with General Cermak. This next slide references Exhibit P2526 at page 61. In the words of General Cermak: "I was responsible for contact with the international community. For that reason, they came to me. The intention was for us to be at their service as quickly as possible and to allow them to sort things out immediately, so they had one contact person." Immediate steps were undertaken to ensure that General Cermak became the central depository and ultimately a black hole for the complaints of the international community. For instance, General Cermak's presidential appointments to his post in Knin was widely publicised in the media, including facts about his high-profile background. Moreover, Croatian authorities and key JCE members were immediately made aware of General Cermak's appointment to Knin. President Tudjman took steps to ensure that the internationals knew that he personally had sent General Cermak to solve their problems on the ground. This is at Prosecution brief paragraph 297 through to 298. This slide references Exhibit D296 at page 20. In the words of President Tudjman: "Tell them I appointed as commander of the Knin garrison Colonel General Cermak, a former minister, a serious man, to solve those matters." General Cermak immediately made contact with the internationals and not only insisted on having frequent ongoing contact with them, but he also demanded that the internationals report all problems to him directly so that he could take action. This slide references Exhibit P2525 at page 50, where General Cermak said: "I asked everybody I ever met that whenever they had information, to inform me about it because I needed the information so I could go take the appropriate steps for people to do something." As requested, the internationals personally and regularly met with General Cermak to inform him directly about the ongoing crimes of looting, arson, and murder being perpetrated against Serbs by members of the Croatian forces. The next slide references Exhibit P2526, page 9, and P2525 at page 12. General Cermak admitted in his suspect interviews that during the relevant period, everything came to him or went through him. Prosecution brief at paragraphs 351 through to 352, and 355. General Cermak intentionally used his rank of Colonel General, matching that of General Gotovina, and his prior status as a senior Croatian statesman in order to attract and focus the attention of the international community, thereby isolating their complaints and insulating senior members of the Croatian Army and government. For the JCE members to effectively carry out their criminal objective, they needed a front man, someone to deal with the internationals, and someone senior enough that the internationals on the ground would not look for someone higher up the Croatian chain of command, either from the Croatian government or from the military. Consistent with this approach, General Gotovina almost immediately insulated himself from the internationals, and directed them to address their complaints about crimes and any other complaints to General Cermak. Prosecution's brief, paragraph 352. General Cermak now argues that he had no authority to fulfil the promises that he made to the internationals that direct action was being undertaken to address the crimes that were being committed by Croatian forces in the wake of Storm. He makes this argument despite the evidence that he was, in fact, the very person who represented himself to the internationals and the media as the person responsible for law and order throughout the area, the person who guaranteed that Croatian forces would abide by international human rights standards, and the person to whom internationals should direct their complaints about HV crimes so that he could take direct action to resolve their protests. It is unreasonable to believe that by some incredible coincidence the formal and informal powers that were granted to General Cermak in Knin precisely mirrored the false assurances that he routinely issued to the internationals in the aftermath of Storm. For instance, General Cermak promised investigations. He promised orders to the military police. He promised disciplinary action. He promised to issue orders to the civilian police. And he promised arrests. To provide just a few examples of General Cermak's own words to the internationals, the first slide references Exhibit P1147: "I have issued an order to the military police to investigate the case and make every attempt to discover the perpetrator." Exhibit P1223, page 1: "I would like to inform you that the civilian and military police services have launched comprehensive operations to uncover and punish the perpetrators of criminal acts against the civilian population." Exhibit P409, at page 2: "I have a list, I have [sic] submitted it to the civilian and military police. This is very embarrassing for me ... I will repeat my orders." Exhibit P2520: "I have submitted a request to the competent commander to launch an investigation and take disciplinary actions [sic] against the perpetrators." Exhibit D618, page 2: "I regret that someone has been behaving inappropriately. Give me the information so I can take measures. We arrest those that [sic] cause trouble." The clear language used by General Cermak gave the intentional and unmistakable impression that General Cermak was taking official action to end the crimes being committed in the wake of Storm. General Cermak told President Tudjman in 1999 that Croatian forces were killing people in the aftermath of Storm and that no one could have prevented it. P1144 at page 7. Such an admission is in stark contrast to the routine statements that were made by General Cermak to the international community and to the media that the situation was under control, as well as his promises to the internationals that efforts had already been made to establish order and discipline within his area of responsibility. See, for instance, P1099 at paragraphs 2 and 5 and 6; and P719, page 4; and the Prosecution's brief at paragraph 353. General Cermak's misleading information and false assurances of official action in response to the protests that he actively solicited from the internationals resulted in the internationals placing confidence in General Cermak to act. As intended, this misplaced confidence effectively stalled the internationals from the timely pursuit of other avenues of redress. General Cermak's obfuscation bought valuable time for the JCE to accomplish its common criminal purpose because it allowed the crimes to continue long enough to drive the remaining Krajina Serbs out of the Krajina, while simultaneously allowing for the completion of the second phase of the process which was to repopulate the Krajina with ethnic Croats. General Cermak clearly had the attention of the media and the international community in Knin, and he took advantage of his position in order to obstruct the international community. General Cermak argues that he was a mere conduit for any information that was exchanged between the internationals and those Croatian authorities who were ultimately responsible for addressing the crime and disorder. The premise that General Cermak's actions were limited to simply passing on information that he received is inconsistent with a number of facts already reviewed but also in light of the following facts. First, General Cermak was granted broad discretion by the president in the execution of his task to deal with the internationals and the media. See the Prosecution's brief at paragraphs 349 to 350, and 333 through 334. During his suspect interview, General Cermak was asked what the president had directed him to say when he dispatched Cermak to Knin to negotiate with the internationals. This slide references P2525 at page 32. General Cermak's response was: "He," referring to the president, "didn't tell me anything. He told me, Go down there, deal with the internationals." General Cermak was also responsible for conducting all contacts with the media and was free to take whatever steps he deemed necessary in this respect. The next slide references Exhibits 2525, pages 13, as well as 32 to 33. In the words of General Cermak: "He," referring to the president, "told me to be in contact with media and to do what is necessary." And: "Nobody ever told me anything, what to say to the media." And: "I had complete freedom there." Second, there was already a conduit system in place; namely, the fully functioning system of Croatian Army liaison officers from the office for the UN and EU. The CALOS were a professional branch of the Ministry of Defence and designed specifically to serve as a conduit between the international community and the Croatian authorities. On 5 August, Minister of Defence Susak ordered General Gotovina to dispatch the CALOS to Knin to work for General Cermak. See Exhibit D1688 at paragraph 10. General Cermak was intentionally inserted as a filter into the CALO system in order to ensure that all complaints about Croatian forces' crimes were funneled directly to him. For instance, internationals reported, this is in reference to Exhibit P147 at page 6: "As per order of the Ministry of Defence, only the Generals Gotovina and Cermak can deal with the international organisations directly. All other official contacts have to pass through the CALOs." Third, General Cermak never told the internationals that he was not the person ultimately responsible for addressing their concerns, and he never told them to take their protests to anyone else, despite his mounting notice of unabated criminal activity. The Chamber should consider Exhibit D618, which are the minutes from a meeting between General Cermak and Mr. Al-Alfi, as well as Forand's deputy, on 7 September 1995, a meeting that was conducted over one month after General Cermak had arrived in Knin, after he had solicited and received countless reports of crimes, after he witnessed the scene in Grubori, and after Forand had accused General Cermak personally of trying to hide the ethnic cleansing being perpetrated by Croatian forces. During this meeting, General Cermak continued to solicit reports of crime. He promised arrests. He promised that HV members would be disciplined. He promised investigations into reported murders. He promised police patrols in response to HV members apparently burning down houses. He promised freedom of movement, and he failed to correct Al-Alfi who referred to the civilian police as "your civil police" and "your men" in conversation with General Cermak. Fourth, given the number of the reports that General Cermak received directly from the internationals, it is revealing that he never personally created a paper trail that reflected the extent of Croatian forces' crimes. This is inconsistent with being a mere conduit. For instance, this slide references Exhibits P2532 at page 43, and P2525 at pages 50 and 120. In General Cermak's words: "I didn't put anything in writing to the president." And: "There was no need to write it," referring to Gotovina. And: "I didn't write any reports to him," referring to Gotovina. The core of General Cermak's liability lies in the fact that he intentionally took no bona fide action in response to complaints about crimes committed against Serbs that he collected from the internationals. Referring to the Prosecution's brief at 356 through to paragraph 362. As pointed out by General Forand during his cross-examination by Mr. Kay, the real problem was Mr. Cermak was, and this slide references transcript page 4251: "... the fact that it was reported and nothing was being done about it." General Cermak had the discretion to say whatever he deemed necessary to the internationals and the media because he was tasked with public relations, which, for him, meant protecting the image of the Croatian government and the Croatian Army in the face of widespread and systematic crimes being committed against the Serb population. See Prosecution's brief at paragraphs 349 through to 350. This next slide references Exhibit 2525 at page 32. General Cermak acknowledged that one of his goals in Knin was: "... to defend the interests of Croatia when there were negative articles and negative questions ..." The Cermak Defence assert that General Cermak admitted that crimes were being committed by Croatian forces and that this fact is inconsistent with the allegation that he was a member of the JCE. The Defence assertion in this respect is misleading, because General Cermak's limited admissions information reflect his contribution to the JCE, and there are two reasons for this. First, General Cermak was careful not to provoke independent international intervention to stop the crimes that were successfully driving out the remaining Serbs from the Krajina. General Cermak could not reasonably deny that Croatian forces participated in the widespread crimes being committed in the wake of Operation Storm, given their obvious participation. Categorical denials of Croatian forces involvement, not only risked alienating the internationals and damaging Croatia's credibility, it also risked the internationals pursuing means outside of the control of the JCE members. General Cermak made this precise point to General Tolj, the head of political administration for Croatia, the Croatian Army, when he reprimanded Tolj for lying in the media about the lack of any HV involvement in crimes, and for saying that all the crimes on the ground were being committed by civilians in uniform. The Chamber should note, however, that General Cermak did offer the identical excuse of civilians in uniforms to the internationals when he deemed it convenient. For instance, P372, and D56, D151, P1223. Second, it is important to consider what General Cermak did not admit in relation to crimes. General Cermak denied accusations that implicated the Croatian Army or the Croatian government in the systematic and widespread crimes being perpetrated against the Krajina Serbs. General Cermak was the apologist for the Croatian state and the Croatian Army, not for individual HV soldiers. He actively solicited and openly acknowledged internationals' complaints about individual members of Croatian forces committing crimes in ordered to neutralise such complaints and to thwart independent action to stop these crimes. General Cermak's role as the government's apologist was confirmed during General Gotovina's briefing of subordinate HV commanders on the morning of 6 August in Knin, see D792, where General Cermak echoed General Gotovina's displeasure at the potentially negative image of the Croatian Army that would be created if the international community was exposed to the chaos, destruction, and undisciplined behaviour of HV soldiers in Knin. This slide references Exhibit D792 at pages 4 to 5. During this meeting, General Cermak noted that Akashi, UNPROFOR and the American, French, and German ambassadors would shortly be arriving in Knin, and he openly stated that was tasked with urgently salvaging the situation and getting things in order because "people will be coming, delegations will be coming, ministers, journalists, to see what the Croatian Army is, to see what the Croatian Army is capable of." The weight of the evidence demonstrates that General Cermak was only concerned with public relations and image control, rather than exerting actual control over the army. General Cermak issued denials to the internationals and the media of any possible higher-level or systematic involvement by the Croatian forces, Croatian Army, or the state in the widespread crimes. This exhibit -- this slide references Exhibit P1223 at page 1. For instance, in response to complaints about soldiers committing crimes, he told the Red Cross: "The acts that you mentioned were perpetrated by individuals who were trying to exploit a brilliant military operation for illegal material gains and for the fulfilment of sick, murderous impulses. Such individuals are criminals, who, dressed in camouflage uniforms, cast suspicions on the honesty of the Croatian soldier and the correct policies of the Republic of Croatia." And to UN reports that men dressed in civilian clothing were found with gun-shot wounds to the back of the head, General Cermak responded that these were lies and insinuations which damaged the reputation of the Croatian Army and the Croatian state. See, for instance, Exhibit P2572 at page 5. And another example is at P504, pages 3 to 4. The Chamber should also consider General Cermak's defensive and aggressive response to General Forand at the accusation that General Cermak was restricting the movement of the internationals in order to obscure the ethnic cleansing that was being committed by Croatian forces. "I do not understand how those under your command are able to control so effectively all movement and, at the same time, almost one month after hostilities, so many houses continue to be burned, driving poor and destitute persons homeless from their land ... "I also request that you stop restricting the movement of the UN elements. If you are sincere about stopping the wanton destruction of property, then I urge you to welcome the independent surveillance of UN teams as a valuable tool in countering banditry." The next slide references Exhibit D145, which was General Cermak's response. Far from admitting the crimes, General Cermak expressed astonishment at what he called General Forand's unfounded allegations, and challenged General Forand to produce evidence of even one single case of Croatian forces burning down a house and driving people from their homes, even warning Forand to be careful about making insinuations without proof. During his cross-examination of General Forand, Mr. Kay highlighted the change in tone exhibited by General Cermak in response to such allegations, even implying that General Cermak may not have written this letter. See transcript pages 4253 to 4257. The next slide is in reference to Exhibit P1144 at page 4. However, in 1999, General Cermak even reminded President Tudjman of General Forand's accusations of ethnic cleansing and explicitly admitted that he had responded in writing to General Forand, telling him to stop playing with insinuations and false stories. General Cermak also talked about his response in his own suspect interview at paragraph -- at Exhibit P2525 at page 57. Given the extent of General Cermak's notice of the number of houses being burned down by HV soldiers, his declaration of astonishment, his demand for evidence, his warning to General Forand about making unfounded accusations, is inconsistent with the image he now attempts to portray of himself as the good-nature, politically disinterested, and impotent messenger for the international community, who is openly admitting the commission of crimes by HV forces. Of course, General Cermak did not limit himself to issuing denials in defence of the JCE. His direct involvement in covering up crimes that were being committed by Croatian forces was exposed by the murders in the hamlet of Grubori, which Ms. Mahindaratne will cover during the next part of the presentation. General Cermak's pledge of political and personal loyalty to President Tudjman in 1999, promising that he would never turn against Tudjman and, "I am here whenever you may need me, for anything. You can always count on me," was precisely the reason that President Tudjman had recruited General Cermak into the JCE in the first place. During this meeting and the ensuing discussion about the ICTY investigation - and this next slide is in reference to Exhibit P1144 at page 6 - General Cermak reverted to his old role as the JCE's apologist and Tudjman's surrogate in the media, offering to wash up the events in question when he spoke with the media about the facts underlying the investigation. "Yesterday I was called by 10, 15 journalists, the BBC, and many local papers. I refused to make any statement. But if you think we should start hammering about that, clear things up and talk about the relationship between us, on which those who accused us found their insinuations, I can wash it up a little." President Tudjman could not resist the offer and reminded Mr. Cermak of the party line. In the same exhibit on the same page, President Tudjman responded: "I don't think you'll manage to avoid answering all the questions. You should say that the accusations are unfounded, then you use all the arguments referring to Knin, mention the shelling of Zagreb in which 100 people were wounded and several were killed. Tell them that the president asked them," the Serbs, "to stay, but their people ordered them to leave, et cetera. Also say that we have instituted legal proceedings against the perpetrators of the crimes that they are mentioning." Your Honours, I am out of time but I would very briefly direct the Trial Chamber's attention to the Trial Judgement in Popovic, where it was found that the acts of an accused in misleading international organisations, where the deception was undertaken in furtherance of a common criminal purpose with a goal of deflecting scrutiny or thwarting interference, that that can be considered as significant contributions in terms of JCE liability. And I refer to the Chamber to paragraphs 1815, 1820, 1822, 2203 in the Popovic trial judgement. Thank you very much, Your Honours. Ms. Mahindaratne will now continue with the Prosecution's closing arguments for General Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carrier. Ms. Mahindaratne, I had on my mind to take the next break at approximately 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. General Markac was assistant minister of interior and the commander of the special police. He played a key role in the execution of the criminal enterprise in his capacity as a commander of the special police forces that committed crimes in Operation Storm and the related search operations. As discussed in our final trial brief and the previous addresses, General Markac actively participated in the Brioni meeting. The Markac Defence argues that the sum total of General Markac's spoken contribution to the meeting consisted of a statement at page 19 of the Brioni transcripts, P461. The Markac Defence argues that it contains no suggestion of General Markac's intent to participate in a JCE. I refer to paragraphs 131 and 132 of the Markac brief. As discussed at length in our final brief, the plan to permanently and forcibly remove the Krajina Serbs crystallised at the Brioni meeting. This morning, Mr. Russo discussed the details of the Brioni plan to use a combination of psychological operations and unlawful artillery strikes to spark off a mass flight of civilians. General Markac actively participated in the meeting. He expressly endorsed it and discussed how his forces would coordinate with the HV in the execution of the plan. He predicted the outcome of the proposed operation in the following terms: "That means that we are going to drive them into a pocket here, and from that point, we can head towards Norac while Norac can head towards Lapac, and we have practically evacuated the entire area. Everything fits in and to all practical purposes we gain with this plan proposed by Mr. Gotovina." Page 461, page 19. The Markac Defence also appears to have failed to notice General Markac's spoken contributions at page 18, 24 to 25, 31 to 32, and particularly, the discussion between President Tudjman, General Cervenko and General Markac at pages 19 to 20 of the transcript. This excerpt of the transcript shows General Markac agreeing to use his subordinates to stage a provocation as a pretext to justify the launch of the operation at President Tudjman's suggestion. P461, pages 19 to 20. The next excerpt shows a continuation of that discussion when Minister Susak suggested a coordinated HV special police effort to stage a provocation. He proposed that two shells be fired at Gospic, a Croatian town, and particularly "an inhabited place -- at an inhabited place. P461, page 30. And as planned, the staged provocation was carried out. I refer to ECMM report dated 2nd August 1995. P831, pages 1 to 2. That is the paragraph numbered 3C of the report. General Markac shared the common criminal purpose to permanently remove the Serb population from the Krajina region by means of the crimes charged. This demonstrated not only by his active participation in the Brioni meeting, but also by his conduct thereafter in the implementation of the decision reached at the Brioni meeting. I refer Court to paragraph 384 of our brief. As discussed at length in our brief, General Markac significantly contributed to the common criminal purpose through a number of acts. He planned Operation Storm and the related search operations in coordination with JCE members. He prepared his subordinates for their tasks. He participated in the planning and ordering of an illegal artillery attack against civilian populated towns, including Gracac and Donji Lapac. He commanded his subordinates during Operation Storm and the related search operations. He was physically present in the field and personally directed his subordinates during the Storm attack, and thereby participated in the crimes. He issued orders to conduct search operations in the aftermath of Operation Storm. And he permitted a climate of impunity among his subordinates in the face of repeated crimes by failing to intervene either to prevent or punish their crimes. And when there was a risk of his subordinates' crimes being revealed, General Markac covered up the crimes by reporting false information and suppressing investigations. The Chamber has already heard our arguments on General Markac's JCE contribution and separate individual liability for the planning and ordering of the illegal artillery attack on civilian-populated towns, and I will not go into that topic. As mentioned by Mr. Russo, General Markac issued a special police attack order for Storm. As the operation progressed, General Markac continued to issue orders to his forces to attack formally Serb-held territory, including Gracac, Otric, and Donji Lapac. I refer to P2385, page 7; P614, page 11; P2384, page 2; and P552, paragraph 34. General Markac personally led these forces into the liberated territory. He was physically present in the field and directed his subordinates. I refer to evidence cited at footnote 1477 of our brief. As the special police forces took control of the territory, they destroyed Serb towns, villages and hamlets they passed by, systematically plundering and burning civilian property. Remaining Serb civilians who were discovered were executed. The evidence cited in support of paragraphs 414 to 426 of the Prosecution's brief and the annexes show the devastation and carnage left behind by the special police forces as they moved north from Gracac, through Otric and Donji Lapac, to BiH border. To illustrate this further, on 5th August, the special police captured Gracac and started looting and destroying private property. On 6th August, they captured Otric, and plundered and destroyed property en route to and in and around Otric. By 11th August, Otric was almost completely destroyed. On 7th August, the special police captured Donji Lapac. En route from Gracac to Donji Lapac, the special police burnt and destroyed as much as 90 per cent of homes and properties situated along that route. As General Markac's deputy testified in response to a question by the Bench, there were no other forces present on those axes of attack, and the special police was the first Croatian forces to advance on those routes. I refer to transcript page 27756. The special police entered Donji Lapac in the afternoon of 7th August and immediately started burning down the place. Donji Lapac was completely destroyed within that night itself and rendered uninhabitable even for purposes of billeting Croatian military units. The special police remained within Donji Lapac until 9th August. I refer to evidence cited at footnote 1514 of our brief. Thus, on 26 August, as mentioned before, at a meeting between President Tudjman, Minister Susak, Generals Cervenko, Gotovina, and Norac, among others, Minister Susak reported that Donji Lapac was completely destroyed. I refer to P470, page 53. At that same meeting, the Gospic Military District commander, General Norac, attributed the crimes to the special police. P470, page 54. Paragraph 422 of the Prosecution's brief addresses the evidence showing the exchanges within the Croatian leadership and the authorities regarding the state of the crimes in Donji Lapac. General Markac discussed the crimes in Donji Lapac with his deputy, Sasic. I refer to evidence cited at footnote 1530 of our brief. However, despite receiving attention even at the presidential level, the destruction of Donji Lapac was never investigated by any Croatian authorities, which indeed reflects the prevailing climate of impunity. Serb stragglers who had the misfortune to be in the way of the special police onslaught were executed. The spate of killings left behind by the special police on their axis of attack and areas of search operations is evidenced by the bodies of civilians recovered along their routes and in the areas captured by the special police. I refer to Annex B of the final trial brief. For example, within Gracac municipality, where General Markac set up his headquarters on 5th August, and which remain as a special police base throughout the indictment period, 53 bodies of civilians were recovered. I refer to Annex B, pages 22 to 33. General Markac's attempt to minimise the special police crimes by making weak attacks against isolated items of evidence is unsustainable. I refer to paragraphs 238, 239, and 258 of the Markac brief. The magnitude of the spate of crimes in areas of special police operations, proof of the presence of special police forces during the time of commission of crimes as discussed in paragraphs 414 to 426 of our brief and the annexes and the -- and the annexes, and the exchanges within the Croatian establishment regarding the crimes cited at paragraph 422 of our brief, corroborate the evidence that General Markac seeks to challenge. The Chamber is also in receipt of photographic evidence of special police crimes in Gracac on 8 August. I refer to P324. As discussed in -- at paragraphs 414 to 423 of our brief, General Markac was present at the crime sites at the time of the commission of the crimes or in its immediate aftermath. As discussed in paragraphs 401 to 404 of our brief, General Markac possessed effective control over the special police forces deployed in the Storm attack and the subsequent search operations. During the Storm attack, he closely monitored forces and they remained under his control throughout the operations. I refer to evidence cited at footnotes 1478 and 1479 of our brief. As demonstrated in paragraphs 466 to 468 of our brief, General Markac failed to intervene to either prevent or punish his subordinates' crimes, despite being present in the vicinity of the criminal activity. Thus, General Markac tacitly approved and encouraged his subordinates to commit crimes. After the completion of the Storm attack, General Markac ordered his subordinates to conduct search operations. The special police conducted a series of operations during August and September which led to a further spate of crimes, as borne out by the evidence cited in the annexes. By late August, special police crimes had been ongoing for weeks without meaningful efforts by General Markac to investigate or punish. He had thus created an environment permissive of criminal behaviour by failing to take measures against crime. General Markac was placed on notice of the possibility that his subordinates were killing civilians, despite which he continued to deploy his subordinates, including some that he knew to be undisciplined and nationalistic, in areas where elderly Serb stragglers remained, without taking precautions. I refer to footnotes 1533, 1544 and 1545 of our brief that cites the relevant evidence. He thus knew of the substantial likelihood that murders would be committed in the execution of his orders. The Lucko Unit, which was considered to be the elite combat unit of the special police, participated in three search operations. One in the area of Petrova Gora on 13th to 14th August; the second in the Plavno valley on 25th August; and the third in the Promina hills on 26th August. They committed crimes in at least two of those operations, on consecutive days, which reflect that this was indeed the order of the day among General Markac's subordinates. Mr. President, I note the time. I -- I am about to move into the area of the crimes in Grubori. I wonder whether this would be an appropriate time to take the break and if so --
