utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, 36 minutes for you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On 25th August, the Lucko Unit murdered five civilians in the hamlet of Grubori, in the Plavno valley, including 80-year-old Milos Grubor who was shot in his bed. They torched many houses, farm buildings and killed livestock. They torched 20 houses, many farm buildings and killed livestock. The following day, 26th August, they torched civilian houses in Ramljane. The Chamber has received a substantial amount of evidence relating to the Grubori crimes, including video footage and photographs. Much attention has been paid to the massacre in these proceedings. However, Grubori wasn't an extra-special event in the context of spate of crimes committed by General Markac's subordinates. It received attention due to one reason and one reason only. A UN human rights action team and a camera crew happened to be present in the vicinity of the crime and reached the hamlet soon after the commission of the crime and video recorded the consequences. If not for their presence, the Grubori victims, too, may have been buried under a blanket of anonymity, like the many hundreds of the other victims in the Krajina. General Cermak, whose primary role was to cloak the crimes and prevent their exposure to the international community, worked in collusion with General Markac to cover up the special police crimes in Grubori. They issued false reports, misrepresented facts and prevented an investigation. The Cermak and Markac Defences do not contest the crime by the special police. I refer to paragraphs 210 and 216 of the Cermak brief, and the propositions made by the Markac Defence during trial at transcript page 28030. General Cermak claims that he was misled about the incident by the special police. He claims that the information he disseminated to the international community and the media was based on the false special police reports and that he had no reason to believe them at the time. General Cermak is on record at least on five occasions, from 26th to 31st August, falsely claiming that the killings and the destruction in Grubori were collateral consequences of combat. He provided different details at different times, depending on where he was and who he was addressing, and provided false assurances to his audience on the truthfulness of his reports. On 26 August, at approximately 11.30, General Cermak made the first public statement regarding the incident to UNTV. I refer to P504. To his interviewer, Richard Lyntton, General Cermak said: "Yes, I know about these events. That happened yesterday ... during the operation itself there was exchange of fire. In the village of Grubori itself, one or two houses were burnt in the operation. One Serbian terrorist was arrested, and one body was found and we believe it was the body of a Croatian Army soldier because he had his hands tied with a wire behind his back. P504, page 1. General Cermak claims that the basis for his statement was General Markac's false report, P576, which was produced after the UNTV, late in the day. General Cermak argues that although the special police false reports were written later, the information may have been conceived earlier. By P576, General Markac reports the death of one enemy soldier and four civilians. By P504, General Cermak refers only to the recovery of one body, with hand tied, presumably of that of a Croatian soldier. In his statement to UNTV, General Cermak does not refer to any other persons being killed in the incident, either combatants or civilians. When specifically questioned, he denied any knowledge of civilians being killed in Grubori. P504, pages 1 to 2. That is because General Cermak's statement was made at a time when all of the details were not known, while General Markac's report, P576 was produced at a time when all of the details, such as the numbers and the identities of the deceased, were known. Otherwise, it would not have made any sense for General Cermak to deny knowledge of the death of civilians to UNTV if that fact was known. General Cermak points out that his reference to a corpse found with hands tied behind the back is reported in special police reports. I refer to argument at paragraph 218, subparagraph 10, of the Cermak brief. This is a reference to special police units of the Split-Dalmatia police administration finding a body with hands tied, reported in a special police report cited by the Cermak Defence. General Cermak argues that this demonstrates that the information he disseminated originated from the special police. Indeed, the Prosecution alleges that General Cermak and General Markac were in communication from the point of receipt of notice of the crimes in Grubori, and agreed prior to the UNTV interview as to what should be reported as the cause of the incident. I refer Court to paragraph 434 of the Prosecution brief. As such, it would be logical for General Markac to pass on factual information in his possession that General Cermak could use to impress his audience with. However, contrary to the Defence argument, General Cermak did not innocently rely on information provided by the special police for his statements. He knew the truth and worked in collusion with General Markac in the fabrication of false reports, false information. For example, none of the special police reports cited by General Cermak to advance his argument at paragraph 218, subparagraph 10, described the body found with the hands tied as that of a Croatian soldier. Neither the special police nor the civilian police informed General Cermak that the body was suspected to be that of a Croatian soldier. I refer to testimony at transcript page 5292. Yet upon recognising the implications of a body found with hands tied, even one that may have been construed to be that of a combatant, General Cermak lied to UNTV to deflect blame from the Croatian forces. In the evening of 26 August, General Cermak's liaison officer, Dondo, Mr. Dondo, submitted a report to him on his observations in Grubori pursuant to a fact-finding mission. I refer to P764. General Cermak read that report at the latest on 27th August morning, on his way to visit Grubori. P764 does not support an allegation of combat and its content indicates clear signs of a crime. Therefore, at the latest when General Cermak read that report, if not before, he knew that what he had advanced to UNTV was false. General Cermak claims in his brief that as a person who had never served in the military, he had no expertise to interpret events from the condition of the village, as far as he saw it, or from Dondo's report. I refer to paragraph 228 of the Cermak arguments. One does not require expertise of any type to comprehend P764. If I may read a brief excerpt. Dondo reported to General Cermak that: "Some 20 houses and many farm buildings were set ablaze, there was no evidence of looting in the houses that remained. "We found five bodies. "300 metres above the village, in a small meadow, was a body of an elderly woman born in 1944. "Next to the woman's body was the body of a man some 35 to 40 years old, Djuro Karanovic, who allegedly came from Belgrade two days ago for the hay-making. "A body of a man, born in 1930, inside a partly burned house, allegedly his wife had brought him from the meadow." "Inside a burned house, a carbonised body, allegedly an elderly woman born in 1905. "Inside a dilapidated house on an improvised upper floor, there lay the body of an old man born in 1915, in a pool of blood, without visible injuries and dressed in a shirt and underpants. "We also noticed a dead cow and a dog in the meadow." That is all General Cermak had to read to know that what he had been advancing up to that point as a cause of the incident was a complete lie. In Grubori General Cermak saw the crime site. The Chamber will recall that a number of witnesses who had no military background testified that what they saw in Grubori did not support the allegation of combat. The Chamber saw photographs and footage of the crime scene. I refer to testimony cited at footnote 1549 and 1659. General Cermak saw the -- that same crime site and now he suggests in his brief that he did not enter the village, that he may not have entered the village. It's a mere suggestion. I refer to paragraph 228 of the Cermak brief. Evidence shows that this is not true, that General Cermak indeed entered the village. The HTV video footage, P2386, recorded on 27th August, shows General Cermak standing in the village, next to burned buildings, where he starts off his statement with the words, "We are in the village of Grubor." In Grubori, having seen the crime site, and having read Dondo's report moments before, General Cermak claimed: "As can you see, there was an exchange of fire ... the village was set on fire. During the action itself, three members of Chetnik groups and two civilians got killed." And then he went on to assure his audience and he said: "I came personally to the village of Grubori [sic] to see for myself the entire course of the action ... so that attempts are not made again to impute something to Croatia, that it was a deliberate arson, that there were deliberate killings ..." P2386, page 1. General Cermak assured his audience the veracity of the truthfulness of the report he just made. A comparison of General Cermak's statement here with the special police force reports, P576 and P563, shows that General Cermak fabricated the information regarding the killing of three enemy soldiers when confronted with the five bodies in Grubori. However, having observed the extent of the destruction, which was difficult to minimise, standing there in Grubori with a TV crew recording the scene, he reported accurately the extent of the damage as the village on fire, as opposed to General Markac who recalls only three cow-sheds and two houses on fire. I refer to P576, page 2, General Markac's report. After the 27th, General Cermak made three further statements to the international community. Due to lack of time, I'll flip through them quickly. On 29th August, at a meeting with General Forand and Al-Alfi, General Cermak maintained the same false version of events. P409, page 3. He reported three renegades and two civilians had been killed, however, minimised the damage as several cattle sheds set on fire. The following day, in response to ICRC inquiries, at P1221, General Cermak responded, by P1222, maintaining the same false allegation of combat. By P1222, General Cermak reported the details as to the number of the deceased, their military/civilian status and their identities consistent with General Markac's false report, P576. This reflects that at this stage, General Cermak and General Markac had started to synchronise their reports with one exception. Having visited Grubori and being aware that the footage of the massive destruction was on video record and accessible to the international community, General Cermak was careful not to minimise what was too obvious so he reported that several cattle sheds and houses were burned. And he assured the ICRC that he had personally visited the area the following day and convinced himself of the truth of the matter. The next day, 31 August, he made a further false report to UNCRO, P603, maintaining the same false allegation of combat. There too he gave the same assurance that he had personally verified the facts he reported. These false assurances show that General Cermak wanted his audience to believe the information he was disseminating. I will move on to General Markac's false report. General Markac reported three different versions of events regarding activities of the Lucko Unit for 25th August. By his first report to General Cervenko, dated 26th August, he reported that the Lucko Unit had not met with combat and no material was recovered by the unit; P575. Then when he learned that the international community was privy to his subordinates' crimes in Grubori, he cancelled this report, P575, and issued the second report, P576. By P576, General Markac reported that the Lucko Unit had met with combat, and in the course of the conflict, one enemy soldier was killed and another was arrested. Due to the use of hand-grenades, three cow-sheds and two houses caught fire and four civilians were killed in the incident. General Markac weaved some of the factual information he had received from Grubori into his false report, P576. Thus he included the identities of some of the Grubori victims in his report, although falsely claiming that Djuro Karanovic was one of the civilians killed in Grubori -- Djuro Karanovic, one of the civilians killed in Grubori, was, in fact, a combatant which is false. By February/March 1996, with the heightened scrutiny of the incident by the international community and being aware that the international community was in possession of evidence that clearly indicated that the incompetence was a crime, General Markac issued his third report, P505. I draw the Chamber's attention to the highlighted section of this report. By P505, General Markac maintained that the special police was in conflict with a group of ARSK soldiers, resulting in the death of one enemy soldier and the arrest of another, but he now made a brand new allegation. He reported that the civilians were executed and houses were burnt by the enemy soldiers before they fled. Even the Croatian government found this new allegation too incredible to advance to the international community, and in June 1996, in a response to Rehn -- Rehn's letter, the foreign minister finally admitted that what occurred in Grubori on 25th August was indeed a crime. He, however, falsely reported on the status of an investigation into the crime when there was none. I refer to P2674. The Markac Defence fails to address the evidence of General Markac personally in -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. Fails to address evidence of General Markac's personal involvement in the fabrication of false reports cited in support of paragraphs 440 to 444, and 450, of the Prosecution's brief, particularly the testimony of Witness Celic. The Markac Defence also fails to address the evidence of General Markac's personal involvement in attempts to destroy ballistic evidence cited at paragraph 453 of the Prosecution brief. An investigation into the Grubori crimes was prevented through the collaboration of many -- many, including, General Cermak, General Markac, Sasic, Minister Jarnjak, and Assistant Minister Moric, amongst others. I refer to evidence cited in support of paragraph 455 of our brief. As discussed in paragraphs 436, 437, 445 to 449, of the Prosecution's brief, General Cermak played the primary role in the suppression of the investigation. In its brief -- in its brief, General Cermak claims he wanted an on-site investigation and that he insisted that an on-site investigation be conducted in front of the media. I refer to paragraph 229, 235, and 257 of the Cermak brief. The following factors, which I will quickly go through due to lack of time, lead to the only reasonable conclusion that the Grubori victims' bodies were disposed of without an on-site investigation following General Cermak's direction to the police, pursuant to an agreement he reached with Minister Jarnjak. Firstly, the Knin police intended to conduct an on-site investigation. D57, page 59; P503, page 27, under seal; and evidence cited at footnotes 1580 and 1639. However, when the Knin police attempted to obtain the assistance of UNCIVPOL to locate the bodies, General Cermak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the French booth is -- states that your reading goes very quickly and it's increasing its speed, it seems. So if you could please --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will try, Mr. President. However, when the Knin police attempted to obtain assistance of UNCIVPOL to locate the bodies, General Cermak advised the police to wait and see. P487, page 15, under seal. On 26 August, General Cermak entertained the dispute between Sasic and the Knin police when Sasic advocated for the disposal of bodies without an on-site investigation, contrary to the intentions of the police. In the course of the dispute, General Cermak did not take a stand on the issue. Paragraph 438 of the Prosecution's brief, and 246 of the Cermak brief. In its brief, General Cermak states that he neither opposed nor was explicitly in favour of an on-site investigation at the time. Paragraph 235 of the Cermak brief. In General Cermak's presence, Sasic telephoned Minister Jarnjak and complained against the police and agitated for disposal of bodies without an investigation. Paragraph 438 of the Prosecution's brief and para 246 of the Cermak brief. After Sasic's conversation, General Cermak himself had a telephone conversation with Minister Jarnjak. Paragraph 438 of the Prosecution's brief and paragraph 246 of the Cermak brief. At 2000 hours that evening, Dondo made an entry in the Knin police log to the effect that victims were killed during Operation Storm and requesting civilian protection to be sent to the site for urgent clearing up of the bodies. D57, page 61; and P764, page 2. The following morning, 27th August, the Knin police met General Cermak for the morning briefing. The police were anticipating an agreement from General Cermak with regard to the civilian casualties in Grubori. P501, page 9, under seal. After the meeting, the police cancelled the on-site investigation that was scheduled and ordered sanitation teams to Grubori for disposal of bodies. P501, page 9, under seal. On 27th August, General Cermak or a member of his entourage, in his presence, requested forensic technicians to send -- forensic technicians sent to sanitise the bodies to place weapons by the bodies to stage a post-combat scene. The forensic technicians refused. Paragraph 446 of the Prosecution brief. On arrival in Grubori, General Cermak requested the forensic technicians who were there for sanitation to conduct an on-site investigation. The forensic technician Bilobrk refused, informing General Cermak that they were not authorised to conduct an on-site investigation, and that -- that this required the presence of an investigative judge, the authorised prosecutor and crime police. When Bilobrk said this to General Cermak, General Cermak became aware, if he didn't know before, that an investigative judge, a prosecutor, and crime police were required for an on-site investigation and that they were not present at the time. He also learned that forensic technicians were neither authorised nor equipped to conduct an on-site investigation. Regardless, General Cermak still persisted with that request. General Cermak then attempted to have forensic technicians carry out their sanitation work, such as photographing and registering the bodies, in front of the TV crew. The forensic technicians rejected that proposition too. These factors clearly reflect that what General Cermak was seeking was not an actual onsite investigation which would have revealed the special police crime. If that was the case, he would requested for the presence of the investigative judge, the authorised prosecutor and the crime police when he was informed of their absence. His intent was to stage an investigation for the benefit of the media present, and through that, to impress the international community that the crime was investigated. As I'm running out of time, Mr. President, I will move to the incident in Ramljane. Despite knowing that the Lucko Unit had committed crimes in Grubori, General Markac deployed the unit the following day in an operation in civilian settlements without taking precautions to prevent any further crimes. As mentioned earlier, the members of the unit torched civilian homes in Ramljane. I refer to paragraphs 456 to 465 of the Prosecution's brief. In Ramljane, General Markac was present by the crime site soon after the commission of the crimes. He saw the houses on fire. I refer to evidence cited at footnotes 1719 and 1722 of our brief. General Markac was concerned that passengers on the Freedom Train, which was scheduled to pass close to the area, may see the smoke. Therefore, he angrily confronted the unit and started to interrogate the suspected perpetrators. In the course of the confrontation, a group leader of the unit, Franjo Drljo, admitted to General Markac that he burnt the houses. I refer to evidence at footnote 1723, 1724, 1725, and 1726. The Chamber heard the testimony of several witnesses who were privy to that dialogue between General Markac and Drljo, cited at footnote 1727 of our brief. In Ramljane, standing by the crime site, Drljo told General Markac that he had set alight to everything, whatever he could or whatever he wanted. I cite testimony of Balunovic at transcript page 28363. Members of the special police are police officers with specialised skills. General Markac and all other members of the special police present in Ramljane, including General Markac's deputy Sasic and the head of the anti-terrorist department Janic, had powers to arrest any person suspected of committing a crime. I refer to the testimony of Janic, transcript 6101 and 6225, regarding police powers of the special police. So all General Markac had to do was arrest Drljo, or direct one of his subordinates present to arrest him, when he admitted to committing arson. However, by his inaction in the face of repeated crimes, General Markac had set a command climate, where he had given clear signals to his subordinates that he approved and condoned their crimes. Having committed crimes with impunity in Grubori the previous day, General Markac's subordinates had no doubt of this fact when they committed crimes in Ramljane, which is demonstrated by Drljo's response to General Markac. In light of all the evidence that the Court had heard of the number of crimes committed by General Markac's subordinates from beginning of the operation, and General Markac's own involvement in directing and encouraging their conduct in the field during the Storm attack and his inaction to punish thereafter, it was obvious that General Markac was not going make an exception in this case. His only response was to withdraw the unit to Zagreb. No further action was taken either to investigate the crime or to sanction any member of the Lucko Unit. Drljo, who blatantly admitted the crimes to General Markac, remained within the Lucko Unit and joined the special police command in due course. The Markac Defence does not address any of this evidence. In fact, they failed to even mention this specific crime in their brief and the events in Ramljane. I will take a quick five minutes of response to General Markac's arguments regarding the Boskoski decision. General Markac argues that once he learned of the serious crime -- the serious nature of the incident in Grubori, he declined to investigate out of comity and respect for the MUP investigative procedures, as he was aware that the police was seized of the matters. Paragraphs 170 and 179 of the Markac brief. In advancing this argument, General Markac partially misstates the significance of the decisions in Boskoski, suggesting that awareness that subordinates have referred a matter or that other competent agencies or persons have initiated investigations or discipline generally excuses a superior's inaction with respect to crimes involving subordinates. Rather, the issue in Boskoski was not one of excuse, but simply whether the superior had satisfied their duty or not. General Markac's conclusion, under customary international law, a superior may satisfy his duty to take necessary and reasonable measures by reporting to competent authorities, omits an important qualification, depending on the circumstances of each case. Relevant circumstances identified by the Appeals Chamber include the degree to which a superior knows that the appropriate authorities are not functioning or the possibility of a sham investigation. I refer to Boskoski Appeals Judgement paragraph 234. In general, the submission of a report will only satisfy the superior's duty where the report is likely to trigger an investigation or initiate disciplinary or criminal proceedings. Boskoski Appeals Judgement paragraph 231, citing Blaskic Appeals Judgement paragraph 72. General Markac's statement, therefore, that an actual investigation is not required where the report concerned should have been sufficient to trigger an investigation is neither logical nor correct in law. Factually, neither General Markac nor any of his subordinates reported the matter to civilian or crime police. Even where the police was seized of the matter, having received a report from other sources, no investigation was initiated. Moreover, the one that was scheduled to take place was prevented by General Markac and General Cermak, in collusion with others. General Markac was an assistant minister of interior. As asserted by him at paragraph 163 of his brief, he was in daily contact with the Ministry of Interior. Six months after the incident in Grubori, and the incident in Ramljane, his deputy Sasic was appointed the assistant minister in charge of crime police. So General Markac was well placed to initiate a criminal investigation, if he so desired, without being perceived as interfering in MUP investigative procedures. Mr. President, if I could take just three more minutes to -- I'm told I have four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you have three more minutes. And I will be very strict.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General Markac appears to argue that he took reasonable measures with regard to the crimes in Grubori when on notice of crimes. He lists a number of such measures at paragraph 175, and surprisingly includes his false report to General Cervenko as a reasonable measure he took to keep his superiors informed of what had transpired in Grubori. Similarly, General Cermak argues that he identified the suspected perpetrators of the crime in his public statements by stating that the incident was caused when special units of the Croatian Interior Ministry had come under fire. I refer to paragraph 261 of the Cermak brief. The Cermak Defence claims that if he intended to deceive the audience, he would have claimed that the perpetrators were unknown. These arguments of Generals Markac and Cermak are without any merit. In misrepresenting the deaths and destruction in Grubori as consequences of legitimate combat, General Markac and General Cermak excluded any prospect for a criminal investigation. If their reports were believed, an issue of a perpetrator would never have arisen. Mr. President, before I conclude I wish to respond to the inquiry made by the Chamber by point 2 of the e-mail of 26 August. The Prosecution confirms the Chamber's understanding of the Prosecution position as set out in footnote 1403 is accurate. Thank you, Your Honours. And I conclude my arguments and give the floor to Mr. Tieger to make concluding remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Misetic, there are 27 minutes left today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, so the record is not confused, I understand that our time has been concluded and no concluding remarks under these circumstances will therefore be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thank Mr. Tieger for clarifying. Good evening, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take that it, at the very end, if you would need five or seven or ten minutes to make final observations --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Much appreciated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I had in my mind, as a matter of fact, that Ms. Mahindaratne has told us how much the Prosecution would still need and then she said 30 to 40 minutes, not knowing that you wanted to make some concluding remarks, but there will be an opportunity for that on Wednesday. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good evening Your Honours. In our opening statement, in March of 2008, we told you about the principle of Occam's Razor, and that all other things being equal, the simplest answer is usually the best one. We told you that we would provide you with the simple, straightforward explanation of the evidence, while the Prosecution would offer you nothing but convoluted conspiracy theories. After two and a half years of trial, we can safely say here today we were right. We told you so. OTP's final brief and now final argument can be summed in one sentence; Your Honours, you cannot believe your own eyes because nothing is as it appears. The Prosecution's brief is written not from the perspective of Prosecutors sworn to an oath to seek justice and the truth, without regard to whether that will result in conviction or acquittal. Rather, it is written from the perspective of the Advocatus Diaboli, the Devil's Advocate. The role of the Advocatus Diaboli in the Roman Catholic church was to argue against the canonisation of a candidate, to take a skeptical view of the candidate's character, to look for holes in the evidence, and to argue that any good deeds attributed to the candidate were fraudulent. That's exactly what the Prosecution has done here. Like the Advocatus Diaboli, the Prosecution argues as if it is their task to take a skeptical view of General Gotovina, to look for holes in the evidence of his innocence, and to argue that every good thing he did to prevent and punish crime was fraudulent. Moreover, the Prosecution's brief, does not allow for the possibility that even one person in the entire state of Croatia did a good thing, or that he did it for the right reasons. It is unfortunate that the Prosecution, very early in this case, lost sight of what its true role should be in the pursuit of justice. We will show you on Sanction now this example from paragraph 7 of the Prosecution's brief. This encapsulates the Prosecution's case: "Tudjman recognised that the international community, although largely not opposed to Croatia's use of force to take back the Krajina, would vigorously oppose its ethnic cleansing. With these considerations in mind, Tudjman and other JCE members took steps to force the Krajina Serbs out of Croatia in a manner that would mask their real intention and later allow the Croatian authorities to plausibly deny responsibility for the exodus of the Serb population." That is their case, Your Honours, plausibly deny responsibility. What is the Prosecution really saying in that paragraph? This was invisible ethnic cleansing. Over 100.000 people, according to the Prosecution, were ethnically cleansed, but those devious Croats did it in a manner that no one could see it. And they say "plausibly deny" because they know that you, the Judges, if you rely on your eyes, will find that not only is it plausible but likely that Croatia did not ethnically cleanse the Serbs. So the message from the Prosecution is: Don't believe your own eyes. It was invisible ethnic cleansing that no one else could see. It was so invisible that even the Serbs themselves who left did not know that the real reason they were leaving was because they felt terrorised by shelling. The evidence demonstrates that the international media descended upon Croatia before and during Operation Storm. It was in Banja Luka and Serbia, interviewing Krajina Serb refugees. And yet not a single international media reported that anyone at the time claimed to have left due to shelling. There is not a single contemporaneous report, UNMO report, NGO report about a single person who claimed to have left Croatia because he left -- because he felt terrorised by shelling. Over 100.000 people fled terrorising shelling, yet the media did not contemporaneously record the statement of a single Krajina Serb who said that. Compare this state of the evidence, Your Honours, to the Prosecution's cases involving the shelling of Sarajevo, and you will be struck by the jarring lack of evidence. Unlike the Sarajevo cases, you have not been provided with the testimony of a single person, whether viva voce, or hearsay, or through a media report, who claims to have lost a family member in the widespread and systematic terrorising shelling of civilians. Likewise, a year later, Human Rights Watch published a report on Operation Storm after interviewing refugees from the so-called Krajina, and that is Exhibit D183, and that entire report did not record a single claim by a single refugee who claimed to have left because of fear of shelling. Four years later, the Croatian Helsinki Committee report also did not identify a single account of a single Krajina Serb who claimed to have left Croatia due to fear of shelling. That's P2402. Serbian intelligence on the morning of 4 August failed to see the invisible ethnic cleansing was targeting civilians, that's D389, in which the ARSK itself reported that the artillery attack was concentrated against "the northern barracks, the ARSK command, the Tvik factory, the railway intersection and others." Despite the fact that the ARSK intelligence specifically reported its assessment on the morning of 4 August, the Prosecution this morning argued that the northern barracks "were not actually targeted, as suggested by the Defence." The Prosecution apparently argues that not only are your eyes deceiving you, Your Honours, but the eyes of the ARSK intelligence operatives, on the morning of 4 August, were deceiving them as well. Alun Roberts didn't see the invisible ethnic shelling -- spreading terror through shelling -- the invisible ethnic cleansing spreading terror through shelling that is seen by this Prosecution trial team. In D712 and D1369, Roberts -- those are media reports of Alun Roberts, on afternoon of 4 August, telling the international media that he -- after having been in the town with General Forand for a meeting with -- at the ARSK headquarters but before the Martic evacuation order, he told the media that there was "no panic amongst the civilians." And that: "It is rather calm, but people inside Knin are concerned what may follow next." He too didn't see the invisible ethnic cleansing. Martic issued the evacuation order, D137, for the entire civilian population in Dalmatia and parts of Lika, yet failed to note the shelling of civilians as a reason for the orders. Instead, he said the reason for the order was the threat to the territory and the threat of encirclement. Martic must not have noticed the invisible ethnic cleansing. Mrksic was on Radio Belgrade on the evening of 4 August. That's Exhibit D106 and D713. And he told Radio Belgrade that the evacuation was taking place to prevent the civilians from being encircled. He too failed to see that the Croatian Army was shelling civilians and that an evacuation was required, as a result. In fact, Mrksic told this Trial Chamber that he thought the preparatory artillery attack on the morning of 4 August, which, in fact, was the heaviest attack because by sunrise, artillery was used for "harassment purposes only," was so precise that he thought it must have been conducted by laser-guided weapons systems. He must not have noticed the ethnic cleansing the Prosecution uncovered 11 years after the war ended. On the 15th of August, the chief of the ECMM mission in Croatia filed his report on Operation Storm and notably stated as follows, at Exhibit D798, page 3, speaking of the reason of the departure of the Krajina Serbs: "Their departure seems to be final. The Krajina authorities, in particular President Martic, encouraged their citizens to leave, stressing that the Croats wanted the territory without its population. Nowhere in the entire report is indiscriminate shelling mentioned as even a possible cause for the departure of Krajina Serbs." UNMO and UNCIVPOL did investigations specifically because of the allegations of indiscriminate shelling, and the results are in P64 and P228, and they found that the shelling of Knin was "concentrated against military objectives." The devious Croats were so good, Your Honours, that both UNMO and UNCIVPOL couldn't find evidence of widespread indiscriminate shelling despite conducting a specific investigation into that allegation. Galbraith and his staff didn't see it. Neither did AG18. Witnesses Flynn and Akashi testified that they went to Knin on 7 August, met the very same UNCRO personnel upon whose testimony the Prosecution relies for its allegation of indiscriminate shelling. Flynn testified that he went to Knin to, amongst other things, specifically examine the allegations of indiscriminate shelling, and when they came away from that meeting with the UNCRO personnel on 7 August, they did not believe that widespread indiscriminate shelling forced the departure of the Krajina Serbs. In fact, at transcript 1308, Flynn testified that, to him, the exodus of the Serbs was orderly and that it was not mass chaos, people running in different directions. Moreover, Flynn and Akashi and the international media flew into Knin on 7 August via helicopter from Split, which means they must have overflown much of Sector South and certainly the Split Military District portion of Sector South. And from the helicopter, Mr. Akashi, Mr. Flynn, and the international media all failed to see the "massive burning" of Sector South that the Prosecution today claimed was taking place. Keep this in mind, Your Honours, all Sector South personnel was reporting to one boss. That was Yasushi Akashi and his office. It was Mr. Akashi's job to review his reports and assess their credibility and then to take action with New York, UN New York, if in fact these reports were credible. Yet Akashi never claimed to the Croatian government that the United Nations believed there was a systematic campaign of burning and looting and killing taking place. In fact, on the 9th of September, Akashi reported to Annan, in D1662, that he told Sarinic he did not believe the Croatian government to be responsible for the crimes. In his witness statement, D1646, Akashi told this Court he did not consider the Croatian government to be behind the burnings, and if he had, he would have raised the issue with Sarinic. It would have been his duty to raise the issue with Sarinic, if he received reports that the government was behind the burning and looting campaign. Your Honours, if the boss of the personnel in Sector South who was receiving these reports did not ultimately agree with the conclusions of his own personnel, and never passed their allegations on to the UN in New York, the Prosecution fails to explain why this Trial Chamber should find that their views of UN personnel in Sector South are not only credible, but that they are the only reasonable explanation of the evidence. Yet the Prosecution insists that it was invisible ethnic cleansing, driving the Serbs out in a way to mask the real intention of the Croatian leadership. The Secretary-General filed a report with the Security Council on the 23rd of August, identified potential reasons for the departure of Krajina Serbs, and did not mention terrorisation through shelling as a possible cause. The Secretary-General must not have noticed the invisible ethnic cleansing in his report of 23 August, which is D90. This is exactly what we told you would happen in opening statements. We offer you the simple, straightforward explanation, while they offer you the convoluted conspiracy theory. You must decide whether to apply Occam's Razor and whether the simple, straightforward answer is a "reasonable explanation of the evidence." If it is, you must acquit. In our opening statement, you will recall that we cited to Judge Schomburg who said, when speaking of the Prosecution's modus operandi: "One can't help getting the impression that an arrest warrant is issued first and only afterwards do the actual investigations begin." At the time of opening statements we could not have known how prophetic Judge Schomburg's observations would be. Indeed, three months into trial and after many of its shelling witnesses had testified, the OTP filed its Rule 54 bis motion, looking for evidence of that which did not exist. There was no indiscriminate shelling. They told you in their opening statement that the indiscriminate shelling was "at the core of the alleged JCE." That's transcript 443, lines 24 to 25. And yet three months into trial they sought the Court's help in trying to find evidence to support this allegation. It is precisely because of the woeful lack of evidence against General Gotovina that the Prosecution has had to change constantly its allegations, like a locksmith with a ring of keys furiously trying to find the right key that will unlock the door to a conviction. These changing allegations are evident from the Prosecution's final brief in which the Prosecution no longer claims, for example, as it did in its pre-trial brief, that "in almost all cases there were no identifiable military targets" in Knin and other towns. That's paragraph 31 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. Now -- that was the Prosecution case and that is the case the Defence was required to meet. Now the Prosecution attempts to hold it against the Gotovina Defence that we pointed out what potential military targets were in Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and other areas. Indeed it was not until November 2008, eight months into trial, that the Prosecution submitted a new expert report from Witness Konings and abandoned the theory that there were virtually no military targets in the so-called Krajina. Next, you were told by the Prosecution, in opening statements, that the Prosecution would prove beyond a reasonable doubt through UNMO assessments that 73 per cent of all houses in Sector South were destroyed after Operation Storm by the 13th of September. That's transcript 461, lines 11 to 13. In its final brief, the Prosecution makes no serious effort to stand by that claim. Today, the Prosecution tried to distance itself from the UNMO assessment, claiming that "the Prosecution is not claiming that the UNMO surveys represent a perfect and flawless account of the destruction." This is telling in the context of the Prosecution's argument that international personnel in Sector South HQ were credible and didn't have a bias. In defending UN Sector South personnel, the Prosecution this morning conveniently ignored other things that the personnel did, including tipping off the Krajina Serbs as to the start of Operation Storm. They ignore the evidence that during the operation, UNCRO was providing intelligence to ARSK commands. Furthermore, the Prosecution now claims, contrary to its UNMO assessment claims, that "larger towns were left relatively intact." And that's paragraph 157. And that it was the "low density rural environments" that suffered damage. That is paragraph 89. Now, in coming up with its theory that larger towns were spared to prevent -- or to colonise the area with Croats but the rural areas were burned down so as to prevent the return of Serbs, the Prosecution has never offered an explanation for why Serbs couldn't return to the larger settlements, or why the burning down of rural areas would have impacted Serbs but wouldn't have impacts Croats living in these areas. You were told in opening statements that Serb civilians were "marched and forcibly transferred out of their hamlets and villages" by Croatian soldiers and "transferred to collection centres or detained with the objective of preventing them from returning to their settlements." That's transcript 465, lines 19 to 23. In its final brief and now final argument, the Prosecution walks away from this claim and makes no mention of collection and reception centres. You were told today that psy-ops and fake leaflets were effective in secretly encouraging Serb civilians to evacuate from Sector South. Yet -- we can show Exhibit 13. Yet when the Prosecution is confronted with the Martic evacuation order, the Prosecution argues the exact opposite. This is paragraph 641 of their brief. "The ineffectual dissemination of the evacuation order reflected its ad hoc nature. Krajina civilians were unaware of the decision or any organised evacuation, or otherwise did not refer to it in describing the circumstances of their flight. Witnesses who would be expected to be aware of this decision, such as police or hospital staff, were not." The Prosecution, of course, can't reconcile how, on the one hand, civilians allegedly received leaflets telling them that there was an evacuation and they should follow the following routes; but on the other hand, when the issue is the Martic evacuation order, then there's no evidence that anyone knew anything about any evacuation. In short, the Prosecution has never been able to find the key to open the door to a conviction because there is no such key. But that obviously won't stop the Prosecution from trying, no matter how absurd the argument advanced may be. One brief matter before we break, Mr. President. The burden of proof. The Prosecution, in almost 400 pages of a final trial brief and now six hours of argument, never once identifies what the burden of proof is, nor do they claim that they have met that burden. In the history of this Tribunal has the Prosecution in any case ever filed a final brief and conducted a final argument without identifying its burden of proof or claiming that it has met that burden of proof. The Prosecution's arguments are not analysed as against the burden of proof. The Prosecution's brief and arguments today are advanced as if we were still at the 98 bis stage; or worse, that all the Prosecution has to do is establish reasonable doubt concerning General Gotovina's innocence. On the contrary, the Prosecution must establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, which the Martic Appeals Chamber said means that: "There is no reasonable explanation of the evidence other than the guilt of the accused." Measured against that exacting burden of proof, it is clear that the Prosecution cannot prove that its interpretations are plausible, let alone that they are the only reasonable explanations of the evidence. Your Honours, this is -- I have a new section. Perhaps this is a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps, then, it is better to start with that tomorrow. We adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow, the 31st of August, 9.00 in the morning, in this same Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 31st day of August, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25
